agroforestry__asset_threat__drought.mechanism: Drought kills the trees of the system and cuts its output. Severe drought can raise tree seedling mortality by 35 to 40% because seedlings cannot match transpiration demands [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_3]. In Colombia, droughts provoked by El Niño between 2015 and 2016 caused significant losses of trees planted by the project, and the area under the most recently planted intensive silvopastoral systems fell by 45 percent in the severe 2019 drought in a survey of 285 farms [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_5, ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4]. In cabruca cocoa agroforests in southern Bahia, Brazil, cocoa tree mortality was 15% during the El Niño event against under 1% normally, 7% of the 317 woody shade trees died, and potential yield fell from 242 to 26 kg/ha, an 89% reduction, still 83% lower nine months after the drought ended [ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_1, ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1]. In Ghana, leguminous shade trees competed with the crop for soil water during severe drought, enhancing crop mortality compared with full sun [ev_tree_canopy_cover_ipccar6ch5_3].
agroforestry__asset_threat__drought.conditionality: This is an establishment-phase risk first, which is the phase a project funds and is exposed to: the measured damage falls mostly on seedlings and newly planted trees [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_3, ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_5], though established cabruca cocoa and its shade trees also died in the El Niño drought [ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_1, ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_2]. Seedling and young-system losses dominate: the Colombian source notes established systems were more drought-resilient than traditional pastures while young ones are vulnerable in their initial years [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4], and one cited study found drought did not increase seedling mortality, though growth was impaired [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_4]. The Bahia cocoa losses carry no unshaded comparator, so they show the damage to the asset, not whether shade made it worse or better [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1]. The Ghana unit is the IPCC chapter's second-hand reading; the chapter writes coffee but the cited study is on cocoa [ev_tree_canopy_cover_ipccar6ch5_3]. The cocoa units are crop-specific and enter the row under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling. Brazil and Colombia are upper-middle income and Ghana lower-middle income, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1, ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4, ev_tree_canopy_cover_ipccar6ch5_3].

agroforestry__asset_threat__extreme_rain.mechanism: The compiler of the Burkina Faso WOCAT sheet on assisted natural regeneration of degraded land judged that the technology copes well with local rainstorm [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1358_2017_local_rainstorm].
agroforestry__asset_threat__extreme_rain.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is a single practitioner rating on a technology sheet from low-income Burkina Faso, with no measured damage, so it does not show the system is undamaged by extreme rainfall [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1358_2017_local_rainstorm]. A second independent source or one measured finding of rainstorm damage would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__asset_threat__fire.mechanism: Accidental fire can damage trees and crops in silvopastoral and agrosilvopastoral systems, and post-fire re-establishment costs could be high [ev_fire_hazard_diasf08_3]. In Senegal, fire is named among the causes of failed regeneration in ageing agroforestry parklands, together with grazing, removal of spontaneous shoots, climate change and the forest code [ev_fire_hazard_seghieri19_16]. The compiler of the Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet judged that the technology copes not well with forest fire or land fire [ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_forest_fire, ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_land_fire].
agroforestry__asset_threat__fire.conditionality: The literature units are statements rather than measurements: the Brazilian unit reports a cited author's comment on producer concern, and the Senegalese unit lists fire among several regeneration threats [ev_fire_hazard_diasf08_3, ev_fire_hazard_seghieri19_16]. The literature sources are upper-middle-income Brazil and lower-middle-income Senegal [ev_fire_hazard_diasf08_3, ev_fire_hazard_seghieri19_16]. The Kenyan coping ratings are practitioner judgements from the same technology sheet, not measured damage [ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_forest_fire, ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_land_fire].

agroforestry__asset_threat__flood.mechanism: Flooding and increased runoff from heavier rainfall could increase soil nutrient loss and erosion within tropical agroforestry systems, and flooding increases tree mortality in cacao agroforests, with older systems potentially more vulnerable [ev_erosion_hazard_watts22_13, ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_6]. WOCAT compilers judged assisted natural regeneration of degraded land in Burkina Faso to cope well with general river flood, and FMNR in Kenya to cope moderately with flash flood [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1358_2017_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_507_2019_flash_flood].
agroforestry__asset_threat__flood.conditionality: The literature units are a tropics review reading earlier studies second-hand; the erosion statement is forward-looking and concerns the system's soil rather than its trees, and the cacao mortality finding is the least robust grade in the review's own scheme [ev_erosion_hazard_watts22_13, ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_6]. A coconut review from Kerala, India, reports second-hand that the coconut palm withstands typhoons and flooding, a no-damage finding for that crop [ev_flood_hazard_kumar22_2]. The coping ratings are practitioner judgements on technology sheets, not measured damage [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1358_2017_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_507_2019_flash_flood]. Burkina Faso is low income and Kenya and India lower-middle income [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1358_2017_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_507_2019_flash_flood, ev_flood_hazard_kumar22_2].

agroforestry__asset_threat__heat_stress.mechanism: The IPCC assessment states that climate change affects agroforestry productivity much as it does individual perennial crops, through increased temperature or water stress, more crop pathogens, changes in pollinator abundance and changes in nutrient content [ev_crop_yield_ipccar6ch5_1].
agroforestry__asset_threat__heat_stress.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is one assessment statement that bundles several climate pressures rather than heat alone, notes limited research on tree crops, reports no measured damage, and records no country or income group [ev_crop_yield_ipccar6ch5_1]. A second independent source or one measured finding of heat damage to the agroforestry asset would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__asset_threat__wind_cyclone.mechanism: A study cited by Philpott et al., comparing abandoned pastures, mixed plantations, abandoned cacao and forests, found that areas with more complex vegetation were least resistant to hurricane damage, losing larger and more trees [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_8]. In the establishment phase, silvopastoral tree seedlings need protection from excess sun and wind, among other threats [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4]. The compiler of the Burkina Faso WOCAT sheet on assisted natural regeneration of degraded land judged the technology to cope well with local windstorm [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm].
agroforestry__asset_threat__wind_cyclone.conditionality: The damage findings are second-hand: the hurricane result is cited, compares abandoned land uses and forests rather than managed agroforestry, and names no location, and the seedling unit lists wind among several establishment-phase needs alongside trampling, herbivory, weeds and fire [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_8, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4]. Against them, the only measured unit, in shaded coffee in Chiapas, Mexico, found minimal vegetation damage from the hurricane, though the unit records its winds as mild [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_7]; a coconut review from Kerala, India, reports second-hand that the coconut palm withstands typhoons [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_kumar22_1]; and the Burkina Faso rating is a practitioner judgement, not a measurement [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm]. Burkina Faso is low income, India lower-middle and Brazil and Mexico upper-middle income [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_kumar22_1, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_philpott08_7].

agroforestry__biodiversity_priority.mechanism: Trees kept in or added to farmland hold more species than the treeless land use they replace. Pooled over 47 publications, silvopastoral systems supported 28.4% higher biodiversity than open pastures; systems with native, unplanted trees were 36.3% above open pasture against 20.9% for planted systems, and invertebrate biodiversity in native-tree systems was 53.7% above open pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_8]. A meta-analysis of cocoa found a significantly higher number of animal species in agroforestry systems than in cocoa monocultures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1], and a review of shaded coffee and cocoa reports, second-hand, a stronger decline in total species richness from agroforestry to plantations (−46%) than from forest to agroforestry (−11%), and bird diversity between 120 and 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. In Colombia, intensive silvopastoral systems are reported, citing earlier studies, to carry four times more birds and 35% higher bird species richness than grass monocultures and 62% higher ant species richness than treeless pastures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2]; a World Bank silvopastoral operation reported increased species richness and abundance, including many forest-dependent and endangered species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]; and silvopastoral projects significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In Niger, FMNR adoption appears to increase tree diversity by between one and three tree species per farm [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1], and Kenyan WOCAT compilers rate plant, habitat and animal diversity as increased on FMNR sites compared with degraded sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_plant_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_animal_diversity]. Farmers in Colombia and Costa Rica see live fences as corridors for fauna and flora [ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6].
agroforestry__biodiversity_priority.conditionality: The gains are measured against degraded or treeless baselines (open pasture, monoculture, degraded sites). Against native forest, silvopasture with native trees held 18.1% lower biodiversity, which marks a ceiling rather than a loss caused by the practice [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12], and the invertebrate-abundance response in native-tree systems was not statistically significant [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_10]. The harm finding in this row is a yield trade-off in Cameroonian cocoa: yields above 1 t/ha did not seem attainable with more than 10 associated species, while yields of about 750 kg/ha were possible with up to 20-23 species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. Design and species matter: a review notes the benefit depends on the variety, abundance and ecological suitability of the tree species used [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_3], and among coffee certification schemes in Nicaragua C.A.F.E. Practices was the only one with a negative impact on tree diversity while the others were positive [ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1]. Several units are second-hand readings or practitioner ratings, the deforestation finding gives a direction with no size and counts as a component of biodiversity rather than a measure of it, and the silvopasture meta-analysis does not name its study countries [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6, ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1]. Coffee and cocoa units are crop-specific; the low- and lower-middle-income fit rests on Niger, Kenya, Nicaragua, Cameroon and the cocoa meta-analysis's mainly lower-middle-income studies [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_plant_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1].

agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__far.mechanism: A meta-analysis of cocoa found a significantly higher number of animal species in agroforestry systems than in cocoa monocultures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1]. A review of shaded coffee and cocoa reports, from a meta-analysis of 74 studies, a stronger decline in total species richness from agroforestry to plantations (−46%) than from forest to agroforestry (−11%), and, from another study, bird diversity between 120 and 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2].
agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__far.conditionality: The shaded-coffee and cocoa review figures are second-hand readings of earlier studies, and the review notes the shaded systems had an overall decline in yield [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. The harm finding is a yield trade-off in Cameroonian cocoa: yields above 1 t/ha did not seem attainable with more than 10 associated species, while about 750 kg/ha was possible with up to 20-23 species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. The richness drop from forest to agroforestry (−11%) marks that shaded systems hold less than forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_1]. All units are crop-specific coffee or cocoa; the cocoa meta-analysis draws mainly on lower-middle-income countries, while the review's studies are not assigned a country [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_1].

agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__inc.mechanism: In Niger, FMNR adoption appears to increase tree diversity by between one and three tree species per farm and tree density by between 12 and 16 trees per hectare [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1]. Kenyan WOCAT compilers rate animal, habitat and plant diversity as increased on FMNR sites, noting that many animal species find safe habitats there and that FMNR sites provide more habitats than degraded sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_plant_diversity]. A meta-analysis of cocoa, drawing mainly on lower-middle-income countries, found a significantly higher number of animal species in agroforestry systems than in cocoa monocultures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1], and in Nicaraguan coffee most certification schemes had positive impacts on a tree diversity index used as a proxy for habitat quality [ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1].
agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__inc.conditionality: The harm finding in this row is a yield trade-off in Cameroonian cocoa: yields above 1 t/ha did not seem attainable with more than 10 associated species, while about 750 kg/ha was possible with up to 20-23 species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. Among the Nicaraguan schemes, C.A.F.E. Practices was the only one with a negative impact on tree diversity, and that finding is read second-hand [ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1]. The Kenyan units are compiler ratings against degraded sites rather than species surveys, and the Niger result counts tree species on farms, not wider biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_plant_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1]. Coffee and cocoa units are crop-specific [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1]. No unit gives a size for the gain in animal or habitat diversity.

agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__inc.mechanism: The Colombian sustainable-ranching completion report attributes increased species richness and abundance, including many forest-dependent and endangered species, to silvopastoral systems at farm and landscape level [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8], and in the Colombian Amazon piedmont silvopastoral projects significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In Colombia, intensive silvopastoral systems held four times more birds and 35% higher bird species richness than grass monocultures, and ant species richness was 62% higher than in treeless pastures in the same landscape [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2].
agroforestry__biodiversity_priority__inc.conditionality: The Colombian project evaluations give no effect sizes, and the deforestation result enters as a forest-cover component rather than a measured biodiversity outcome [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]. The evidence is from upper-middle-income Colombia only. The Colombian bird and ant figures are earlier studies cited in a CATIE edited volume [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: Trees added to cropland and pasture store carbon in their biomass and raise soil carbon. IPCC assessments state that agroforestry accumulates between 0.59 and 6.24 t ha–1 yr–1 of carbon above-ground at field scale, with below-ground carbon often 25% or more of the gains, and describe large mitigation benefits from increasing carbon sinks in vegetation and soils [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6ch5_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccsrccl6_1]. Meta-analyses report more soil organic carbon under agroforestry than under controls or crop monocultures in sub-Saharan Africa (RR 1.2), the tropics (overall effect size 1.21) and West African fields with shrubs and trees (+ 20 to 75%) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1]; a global synthesis for IPCC Tier 1 coefficients found a mean stock change factor of 1.25 for croplands converted to agroforestry [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_1]. East African agroforestry systems stock an average of 24.2 Mg C ha−1 in biomass and 98.8 Mg C ha−1 in the soil [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muthuri23_1]. In shaded tree crops, total biomass carbon in cocoa agroforestry is on average 2.5 times higher than in a monoculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1], a coffee agroforestry farm in Costa Rica stored a mean 3.6 t C/ha/yr over eight years of eddy-covariance measurement [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5], and shaded coffee plots held 29,8 Mg ha-1 more above-ground biomass carbon than full-sun plantations [ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6]. In Costa Rican silvopasture, carbon storage potential was 1.2 to 4.5 Mg ha-1 yr-1 against less than 1 Mg ha-1 yr-1 in pastures without trees [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. In Ethiopia, regeneration projects at Humbo and Soddo report 181,650 and 94,817 tonnes of CO2 sequestered since 2007 [ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_12], and WOCAT practitioner ratings record FMNR in Kenya sequestering carbon in biomass and raising soil organic matter, with a large soil organic matter gain rated in Burkina Faso [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_507_2019_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_1358_2017_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C]. Avoided deforestation by silvopastoral projects in Colombia, compared with control properties, enters as a forest-cover component with no carbon quantity attached [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: The starting land use decides the sign: converting forest to agroforestry gave a stock change factor of 0.89, a soil carbon loss and the harm finding in this row, and the soil carbon change rate for grassland converted to agroforestry (0.23 t C ha−1 yr−1) was not significantly different from zero [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_3]. Measured on-farm comparisons also sit close to no effect in places: soil organic C did not differ significantly under and outside Faidherbia albida canopies in Ethiopia [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1]; in Malawi soil C under a Tephrosia intercrop was 1.57 against 1.46 under monoculture maize, a trend with P value = 0.10 [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1]; the cocoa meta-analysis found no significant differences in soil chemical properties between agroforestry and monoculture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_niether20_1]; and certified shade coffee in Nicaragua had positive but not statistically significant impacts on above-ground carbon stocks [ev_carbon_sequestration_castle21s_1]. Much of the rest is assessment-level or modelled (global technical and economic potentials, per-hectare mitigation densities), and the project totals carry no per-hectare or per-year denominator [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. Only a minority of units state a size, and the pooled size rests on soil organic carbon response ratios, a component of sequestration rather than a rate; the IPCC notes regional estimates are scant and options differ by geography [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kuyah19_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_7]. WOCAT units are compiler judgements, not measured stocks [ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_1358_2017_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C]. Coffee, cocoa and coconut units are crop-specific [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_kumar22_1].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: Spanish-language reviews report that intensive silvopastoral systems capture more carbon, offsetting livestock methane, that silvopastoral systems established from degraded natural woodland increase above- and below-ground carbon stocks, and that in a Colombian climate-smart prioritisation only tree-improved pastures and live fences showed a positive effect on the mitigation pillar [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: All three are cited secondary statements without effect sizes; among them an expert prioritisation matrix rather than a measurement [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6]. They come from Colombia and Latin America generally [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: Shade and timber trees in tree-crop systems add biomass carbon over the crop alone. Total biomass carbon in cocoa agroforestry, including cocoa and shade trees, is on average 2.5 times higher than in monoculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1]. In Costa Rican coffee agroforestry, an eight-year eddy-covariance carbon balance of trees, coffee, litter and soil gave a mean storage of 3.6 t C/ha/yr, and shaded coffee plots held 29,8 Mg ha-1 more above-ground biomass carbon than full-sun plantations [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6]. East African perennial tree-crop systems hold 29.9 Mg C ha−1 of above-ground carbon [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4], and modelled Ethiopian enset-coffee and tree-coffee systems translate to biomass carbon of 139.5 and 153.4 Mg/ha [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_6]. A coffee review reports agroforestry can improve soil organic matter by 20–35% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_patil25_5].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: The soil side is weaker than the biomass side: the cocoa meta-analysis found no significant differences in soil chemical properties between agroforestry and monoculture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_niether20_1], and the coffee soil figure is a review's second-hand reading [ev_soil_organic_carbon_patil25_5]. The Costa Rican coffee units are from a high-income country, and the shaded-coffee figure is cited from earlier work [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6]; the Ethiopian figures are model outputs cited second-hand [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_6]. The East African and Ethiopian figures are stocks, not annual rates [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4]. Coffee, cocoa and enset units are crop-specific; the low- and lower-middle-income fit rests on the cocoa meta-analysis and the East African review [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: In Costa Rican coffee agroforestry, an eight-year eddy-covariance carbon balance of trees, coffee, litter and soil gave a mean storage of 3.6 t C/ha/yr, and shaded coffee plots held 29.8 Mg ha-1 more above-ground biomass carbon than full-sun plantations [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6]. In Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems had a carbon storage potential of 1.2 to 4.5 Mg ha-1 yr-1, against less than 1 Mg ha-1 yr-1 in pastures without trees [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1].
agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.conditionality: These units come from high-income Costa Rica, from coffee and silvopastoral systems, and the shaded-coffee and silvopasture figures are cited secondary results [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. They lie outside the LIC/LMIC target income band and should not be transferred to LIC/LMIC tree-crop systems without local evidence [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6].

agroforestry__carbon_sequestration_poten.mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings, trees on farms raise both biomass and soil carbon. Across sub-Saharan Africa, agroforestry improved soil organic carbon over controls (RR 1.2) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kuyah19_1]; in West African fields, the presence of shrubs and trees had an overall positive but variable effect on soil total C (+ 20 to 75%), ascribed to litter deposition and sediment trapping [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_2]; and a meta-analysis cited for Senegal reports 46 per cent more soil organic carbon under Faidherbia canopy than outside it [ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. East African agroforestry systems stock an average of 24.2 Mg C ha−1 in biomass and 98.8 Mg C ha−1 in the soil, with much of the above-ground carbon held in homegardens, perennial tree-crop systems and trees on boundaries [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muthuri23_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_5]. Total biomass carbon in cocoa agroforestry is on average 2.5 times higher than in monoculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1]. In Ethiopia, regeneration projects at Humbo and Soddo report 181,650 and 94,817 tonnes of CO2 sequestered since 2007 [ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_12]. A multi-country restoration programme observed an overall relative increase of 3% in soil organic carbon over baseline and a positive, significant association between trees scaled up on-farm and changes in soil organic carbon [ev_soil_organic_carbon_rgaf23_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_rgaf23_4]. Modelled regional potentials put agroforestry at 0.19 GtCO2eq yr−1 in Africa and the Middle East and 0.37 GtCO2eq yr−1 in Asia and the developing Pacific at up to $100/tCO2eq [ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_3].

agroforestry__cross_family__production_g.mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis reports crop yield under agroforestry about twice that of non-agroforestry controls in the humid zone, and a pantropical meta-analysis finds higher soil nitrogen stocks than in crop monocultures, used here as a component [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. A meta-analysis cited in Arslan et al. (Branca et al.) associates agroforestry techniques with a 69% increase in cereal yields across the studies it consulted [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. IPCC assessments attribute higher land-equivalent ratios and large food-production benefits to well-planned agroforestry, and a cited review reports agroforestry systems 36-100% more productive than monoculture [ev_crop_yield_ipccar6ch5_8, ev_crop_yield_ipccsrccl6_3, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_12]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers in an agroforestry project improved farm productivity on average against a control group [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1].
agroforestry__cross_family__production_g.conditionality: A systematic review's pooled crop-yield effect has a confidence interval spanning zero, an integrative review counts 15 of 21 studies favouring agroforestry and 5 favouring monoculture, and another review notes trade-offs between crop intensification and ecosystem services in most agroforestry [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_1, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_1, ev_crop_yield_vannoordwijk21_7]. The cited 69% cereal-yield figure reaches this row second-hand through Arslan et al.: the citing text does not describe the agroforestry techniques further and reports no significance [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. The pooled magnitude combines a crop-yield and a soil-nitrogen response ratio [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. The Lower Nyando productivity gain had large standard errors and was not significant [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. Livestock yield under linear agroforestry (alleys and windbreaks pooled) in a global review did not differ from the control: a 0.3% reduction with a 50–50 split of positive and negative responses over 36 paddock years [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_13].

agroforestry__cross_family__rural_povert.mechanism: IPCC assessments link agroforestry to food security and household income through diversification of production, East African agroforestry supplies fodder, food, firewood and income that act as safety nets in climate shocks, and calliandra fodder raised dairy farmers' net income in Kenya and Uganda [ev_food_security_ipccar6ch5_7, ev_food_security_ipccsrccl6_6, ev_food_security_muthuri23_1, ev_household_income_kiptot11_1]. Brazilian agroforestry viability studies report positive financial indicators, and diversifying production and income is said to reduce farmers' vulnerability to commodity price volatility [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_1, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_7, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_8, ev_household_income_seghieri19_8]. In Rwanda, tree products are a safety net: food-insecure farmers more often sold tree products for income than food-secure farmers, and tree density was positively associated with food security in some agroecologies [ev_household_income_ndoli21_1, ev_food_security_ndoli21_1]. In Nyando District, Kenya, agroforestry-project households typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, sold fuel wood and timber to buy food during the drought, relied on tree fruit when floods washed crops away, and in Lower Nyando held more livestock wealth than control households [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_2]. In a Mozambique carbon-forestry scheme promoting almost exclusively agroforestry, overall household income was generally increased [ev_household_income_lasco14_1]. A global systematic review of nature-based solutions for food security counts three cited population-survey studies finding positive results in food access where agroforestry was applied in southern Africa, Brazil and China over periods of up to 20 years [ev_food_security_nguy24n_1]. In the Nepal mid-hills, after a market-oriented agroforestry project of fodder-tree hedgerows and understorey cash crops, bundled with marketing support, training, seed subsidies and organic fertiliser, the share of participating households below the poverty line dropped from 48 % to 34 %, the share that was food sufficient rose from 52% to 69%, and the average farm-income figure rose from 37 to 48 percent, mainly from understorey crops, while off-farm income changed by -9% [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1, ev_food_security_pandit19_1, ev_household_income_pandit19_1].

The Rwandan effect varied by agroecology: more trees went with higher food security in Congo Nile but lower food security in the Buberuka Highlands [ev_food_security_ndoli21_2]. The Lower Nyando livestock-wealth difference, used by the authors as an income surrogate, was not significant at conventional levels, and the timber-sales and flood-fruit findings are farmer-reported [ev_household_income_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1]. The Mozambique result is a review citation without an effect size [ev_household_income_lasco14_1]. The food-access vote count comes from a low-tier systematic review that included only studies showing improvement in at least one food-security dimension, so its positive count is guaranteed by its inclusion rule and says nothing about studies that found no benefit; of its three cited studies, one is a life-cycle assessment rather than a population survey and another is not clearly agroforestry [ev_food_security_nguy24n_1]. The Nepal results come from a bundled project and are not credited in full to the trees: they are a before-and-after recall survey of participating households with no control group, and the share of the bundle due to agroforestry is not stated [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1, ev_food_security_pandit19_1, ev_household_income_pandit19_1].

agroforestry__cross_family__soil_erosion.mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis found agroforestry five and ten times better than controls for runoff and soil loss respectively [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. A pantropical meta-analysis found agroforestry trees reduced soil erosion by 50% against crop monocultures, IPCC assessments describe agroforestry limiting erosion and stabilising soils with perennial vegetation, and farmland with agroforestry is reported more resilient to heavy rainfall through a 20–50% decrease in runoff, used here as a component [ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_ipccar6ch5_5, ev_erosion_hazard_ipccsrccl6_2, ev_runoff_reduction_dobhal24_2]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1].
agroforestry__cross_family__soil_erosion.conditionality: The sub-Saharan authors warn the very large effect sizes could reflect publication bias, and Regreening Africa observed no large overall change in erosion prevalence [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_3]. The IPCC statements are assessment-level, and several units are review statements without effect sizes [ev_erosion_hazard_ipccsrccl6_5, ev_erosion_hazard_watts22_12, ev_erosion_hazard_santos25_2]. The Lower Nyando erosion finding is farmer-reported, not measured [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1].

agroforestry__cross_family__water_stress.mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis finds that agroforestry improved infiltration and soil moisture content compared to the control, with a weighted response ratio of 1.6 for soil moisture across 62 observations from 27 studies, and 70% of soil-moisture observations above RR 1 [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. Wetter soil under trees eases the crop's water stress. A cited statement adds that rainfall over agricultural land can shift with continental land cover, increasing with more upwind tree cover [ev_water_regulation_vannoordwijk21_4].
agroforestry__cross_family__water_stress.conditionality: The meta-analysis pools agroforestry practices without separating soil depth, so it cannot show whether trees and crops compete for deeper water; the Faidherbia parkland evidence that does show subsoil depletion sits in the regeneration-farmland row [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. The effect on infiltration was greater than that on soil moisture [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. The upwind-rainfall shift is a continental-scale effect from a secondary citation, not a field-scale one [ev_water_regulation_vannoordwijk21_4]. Groundwater-recharge findings are carried in the agroforestry catchment water yield rows.

agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.mechanism: The only quote is a maladaptation example: planting shade trees that damage existing infrastructure during storms [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].
agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.conditionality: This is a typology example from a Latin American adaptation review, not a measured effect on livelihoods or crops, and no country or income group is recorded, so fit to the LIC/LMIC target cannot be checked [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. No unit is from an agro-pastoral system; the evidence is applied to agro-pastoral systems by default [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].

agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.mechanism: Trees cut both ways in storms. A smallholder agroforestry review notes that trees on farm serve as windbreaks and shelterbelts and are used to rebuild property damaged during storms [ev_windbreak_protection_lasco14_1]. A Latin American adaptation review gives planting shade trees that damage existing infrastructure during storms as an example of increased vulnerability [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].
agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.conditionality: The sides differ in what is exposed: the protective statement concerns sheltering and rebuilding on the farm, while the harmful example concerns trees falling on or damaging existing infrastructure [ev_windbreak_protection_lasco14_1, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. Placement relative to buildings and infrastructure is therefore the design point the evidence implies. Neither unit is a measured effect on livelihoods or crops: one is a typology example and the other a narrative review statement, and neither records a country or income group, so fit to the LIC/LMIC target cannot be checked [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5, ev_windbreak_protection_lasco14_1].

agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.mechanism: The only quote is a maladaptation example: planting shade trees that damage existing infrastructure during storms [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].

No unit is from an irrigated cropping system; the evidence is applied to irrigated cropping systems by default [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].

agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.conditionality: This is a typology example from a Latin American adaptation review, not a measured effect on livelihoods or crops, and no country or income group is recorded, so fit to the LIC/LMIC target cannot be checked [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. No unit is from a rainfed cropping system; the evidence is applied to rainfed cropping systems by default [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].

No unit is from a mixed crop-livestock system; the evidence is applied to mixed crop-livestock systems by default [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].

agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.conditionality: This is a typology example from a Latin American adaptation review, not a measured effect on livelihoods or crops, and no country or income group is recorded, so fit to the LIC/LMIC target cannot be checked [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. No unit is from a pastoral rangeland system; the evidence is applied to pastoral rangeland systems by default [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].
