agroforestry__cross_family__wind_cyclone.conditionality: This is a typology example from a Latin American adaptation review, not a measured effect on livelihoods or crops, and no country or income group is recorded, so fit to the LIC/LMIC target cannot be checked [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. No unit is from a tree-perennial system; the evidence is applied to tree-perennial systems by default [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5].

agroforestry__drought__agro_pastoral.mechanism: Trees and live fences carry livestock through drought as a fodder reserve: trees were the main source of animal feed and milk production for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought, and live fences of Gliricidia sepium, Leucaena leucocephala and similar species supply high-quality fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. During drought, understorey crop yield can be higher than in an open system even under intense shade, silvopastures are credited with better water infiltration rates, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].
agroforestry__drought__agro_pastoral.conditionality: The Zambian, US and Sahelian parkland units come from agro-pastoral systems, and the US silvopasture unit is high-income evidence that names infiltration rather than a drought outcome [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]; the understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, as tree shade can lower understorey yields under normal rainfall [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. A Nigerian model study, used as an income proxy, found no significant impact on agroforestry household net revenues under a simulated warmer, drier climate [ev_household_income_watts22_14], and the Kenyan FMNR unit is a compiler rating on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. Against the benefit, earlier work cited in a temperate alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of tree–crop competition; it is a cited, high-income cropping result applied here by default [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. The Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper, and the parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1].

agroforestry__drought__agro_pastoral__in.mechanism: A US silvopasture study lists better water infiltration among silvopasture's services, used here as a soil-water component of drought [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. Against this, earlier work cited in a temperate alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of tree–crop competition [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3].
agroforestry__drought__agro_pastoral__in.conditionality: This is a high-income scope row resting on two second-hand statements that point in opposite directions, so no clear effect can be drawn [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. The silvopasture statement does not mention drought, and the shelterbelt finding concerns crop yield rather than an agro-pastoral outcome, applied here by default; neither transfers directly to LIC/LMIC agro-pastoral systems [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3].

agroforestry__drought__all.mechanism: In two Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, farmers said deep-rooted trees reach water from deep down and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought, citing deep root systems that use a greater soil volume for water [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Trees also share deep water and act as a fodder reserve: hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots, millet with the shrub Guiera senegalensis in the Sahel produced over 900% more biomass under water stress, and trees were the main source of feed and milk for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14]. In an induced drought in eastern Canada only the monocrop lost yield, agroforestry biomass in the Brazilian semi-arid varied far less over 4 years than conventional systems, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Nyando District, Kenya, households in an agroforestry project typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, and many farmers reported selling fuel wood and timber from their trees to buy food during the drought [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. Live fences of species such as Gliricidia sepium and Leucaena leucocephala supply livestock fodder in the dry season, when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. For shaded coffee and cocoa: in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest, the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; and reviews cite a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season and low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11].
agroforestry__drought__all.conditionality: The class comes from the sub-practice vote, not the pooled units: the regeneration-on-farmland, planted silvoarable and silvopastoral cells read as benefits, while the linear-boundary and shaded perennial-crop cells are conflicting. Trade-offs pull the other way: tree–maize competition for soil water in Kenya can lead to crop failure, and a Senegal review finds no clear consensus on windbreak hedges in drought, with some studies reporting higher yields in drier years and others harm to rainfed crops [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. The understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, since tree shade can lower understorey yields under normal rainfall, and the Kenyan household link to perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5]. Several units are proxies, bundled or rated rather than measured: a Nigerian model found no significant drought impact on household net revenues, the Canadian and US units are high-income evidence, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating [ev_household_income_watts22_14, ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. A cited temperate finding of greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years adds to the counter-evidence, the German soil-water difference was not significant everywhere and is high-income evidence, and the Nyando timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper, and the parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. The Latin American silvopastoral units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The Ethiopian Faidherbia result is a drought-year comparison reported as an 'up to' figure; the same study reports its normal-season gain separately, so this hazard-year gain is not the usual yield effect [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In shaded cocoa and coffee the evidence is split: reviews cite that under warmer, water-limited conditions competition between trees and cacao for scarce soil water can reduce soil moisture and cacao yields below those of open-sun farms, that drought caused greater water loss in cacao agroforests than in open-sun cacao because trees and cacao both transpire, and that intercropping may compete for soil moisture during drought [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_9, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]; and in the Ghana experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline and only partly compensated for it [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in the extreme climate shocks [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; and across cabruca cocoa farms in southern Bahia, Brazil, drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2]. These harm findings are second-hand readings in reviews. The cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; the Ghana shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2].

agroforestry__drought__all__income_group.mechanism: In an induced-drought experiment in an eastern Canadian soybean-intercropping agroforestry system, crop losses occurred only in the monocropping system [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. A US silvopasture study lists better water infiltration among silvopasture's services, used here as a soil-water component of drought [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9].
agroforestry__drought__all__income_group.conditionality: This is a high-income scope row: all units come from Canada, Germany, the USA or temperate settings, outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. Against the benefit, earlier work (Kowalchuk and Jong) cited in the German alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of tree–crop competition [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. The Canadian result is reported second-hand in an IPCC chapter, which also notes N-fixation declined in both systems, the German soil-water result is a component measure that was not significant at all positions, and the US unit is a background statement that does not mention drought [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9].

agroforestry__drought__all__income_group.mechanism: In two Isiolo County communities in Kenya, a household survey and interviews conclude that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought: households listed agroforestry as important for their livelihood during drought, in Burat households practising it mostly said droughts were less frequent while most households without it said the opposite, 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind, and farmers explained that deep roots let trees get water from deep down so they keep producing fruit when there is no rain [ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Trees also act as a fodder and cash reserve: in southern Zambia trees were the most important source of animal food and milk production during drought, in Senegal's sylvopastoral zone tree leaves, fruits and pods make up about 40 per cent of cattle diet and 80 per cent of small-ruminant diet before the rains, and in Nyando District, Kenya, agroforestry-project households typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods while many farmers sold fuel wood and timber to buy food during the drought [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts, and in Ethiopia's sustainable land management programme stakeholders rated 14 of 22 cases as having a substantial or high effect on drought vulnerability, naming income from commercial agroforestry as one route that reduced vulnerability in some communities [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In a throughfall-exclusion experiment in Ghana, cocoa dry bean yield was 12 to 45% higher under shade than in full sun at every level of rainwater suppression, and in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly positive for coffee yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1].
agroforestry__drought__all__income_group.conditionality: Tree–crop competition can reverse the effect: a review cites Kenyan trials in which competition with Grevillea robusta for limited soil water delayed maize flowering and could lead to crop failure, an FAO review for Senegal finds no clear consensus on windbreak hedges in drought (some studies report higher yields near hedges in drier years, others harm to non-irrigated crops), and a model cited in a review found no significant effect on Nigerian agroforestry household net revenues under 1°C warming and a 7% fall in annual rainfall [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. In Kinna, drought perceptions did not differ between households with and without agroforestry [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5], and the severe-drought evidence is a cited Honduran observation with no measured size [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. The Kenyan resilience findings come from a single survey and are perception-based, the Zambian, Senegalese and competition findings are secondary citations in reviews, the Ethiopian rating credits a bundled programme rather than agroforestry alone, the FMNR unit is a compiler rating, and the Nyando timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper, and the parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In the Ghana cocoa experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced decline, and the Ethiopian coffee study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in extreme climate shocks; both are among the no-benefit results in this row [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. The Ghana shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so its transfer to agroforestry is borderline, and the cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific, entering because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]. The Ethiopian Faidherbia result is a drought-year comparison reported as an 'up to' figure, not the usual yield effect [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2].

agroforestry__drought__cropping_irrigate.mechanism: Agroforestry raised soil moisture over controls (RR 1.6) in a sub-Saharan African meta-analysis, and a cited synthesis reports perennial trees added to cropland raise rainfall infiltration by 59% [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_10]. Live fences supply fodder in the dry season when pasture is scarce, and shaded understorey crops can yield more than open systems under drought [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. In Ethiopia, income growth through commercial agroforestry is named as one option that reduced drought vulnerability [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4].
agroforestry__drought__cropping_irrigate.conditionality: The quantified evidence is soil water, a component proxy for drought impact; the Ethiopian result is for a bundled land-management programme based on stakeholder responses, and the other units are reviews citing other studies [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_10, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. Only the Ethiopian unit names a country (low income); the rest are regional or pantropical reviews [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. No unit is from an irrigated cropping system; the evidence is applied to irrigated cropping systems by default [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_10, ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1].

agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed.mechanism: On rainfed cropland the evidence divides on whether trees add water the crop can use or compete with the crop for it. Hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots, and in the Sahel millet intercropped with the shrub Guiera senegalensis produced over 900% more biomass under water stress [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1]. In an experimentally induced drought in eastern Canada, crop losses occurred in the monocrop only, not in the soybean intercropping agroforestry system, and during drought understorey crop yield can be higher than in an open system even under intense shade [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]; the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2].
agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed.conditionality: The sub-practices disagree, so the roll-up states conflicting evidence. On the gain side, regeneration-based farmland holds the stronger result and reads as a benefit throughout: Sahelian parkland trees make deep soil moisture available to crop roots, the FMNR compiler rates drought impacts as mitigated, Quesungual crops withstood the 1997 drought, and Ethiopian wheat under Faidherbia albida out-yielded open-field wheat in the El Niño year, a hazard-year result kept apart from the study's normal-season gain [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. On the conflicting side, planted silvoarable systems pair gains (the Canadian induced drought, the Sahelian millet–Guiera result, German alley-cropping soil water) with a reversal, Kenyan maize under Grevillea robusta, where competition for limited soil water delayed flowering and can lead to crop failure [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_crop_yield_watts22_10]; and boundary plantings pair a live-fence fodder role in drought with greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years and a Senegal review that finds no consensus on windbreak hedges in drought [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. What separates the sides in the units' own words is whether tree roots reach moisture the crop cannot, or compete with the crop for limited soil water close to the trees. The understorey drought-year result and the Nigerian income model sit outside the voting sub-practices: the understorey benefit reverses under normal rainfall, and the income model found no significant drought effect [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. The Canadian result is high-income temperate evidence, the live-fence fodder unit is a pantropical review, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating rather than a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The German soil-water difference was not significant at all positions and is high-income evidence, and the Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].

agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed_.mechanism: In an experimentally induced drought in eastern Canada, crop losses occurred in the monocrop only, not in the soybean intercropping agroforestry system [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1].
agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed_.conditionality: The evidence pulls both ways: earlier work cited in the German alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of tree–crop competition [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. This is a high-income temperate scope row (Canada, Germany) outside the LIC/LMIC target; the Canadian result is reported second-hand in an IPCC chapter, and the German soil-water result is a component measure that was not significant at all positions [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1].

agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed_.mechanism: The evidence for rainfed cropping points both ways. A review cites Kenyan trials in which maize grown with Grevillea robusta competed with the trees for limited soil water, which delayed maize flowering and development and could lead to crop failure [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10]. Against this, the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts, and in Ethiopia's sustainable land management programme income growth through commercial agroforestry was named as one option that reduced drought vulnerability in some communities [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].
agroforestry__drought__cropping_rainfed_.conditionality: An FAO review for Senegal reports no clear consensus on windbreak hedges in drought: some studies find higher yields near hedges in drier years, while others judge the hedges could harm non-irrigated crops; and a model cited in a review found no significant effect on Nigerian agroforestry household net revenues under 1°C warming and a 7% fall in annual rainfall [ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. Whether trees help or hurt the crop in drought turns on how strongly they compete for limited soil water [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10]. Much of the pool is second-hand: the competition result and both review findings are secondary citations, the Ethiopian rating belongs to a bundled programme (terracing, bunds, area closure, small-scale irrigation and agroforestry) rather than agroforestry alone, the FMNR unit is a compiler rating, and the source of the Nigerian model notes its weak fit may understate impacts [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. The Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].

agroforestry__drought__mixed_crop_livest.mechanism: In mixed crop–livestock settings the evidence points the same way, though few units say how large the effect is, so the class is a slight reduction in drought impact. In two Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, farmers said deep-rooted trees reach water from deep down and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14]. In the Brazilian semi-arid, agroforestry biomass productivity varied far less over 4 years than conventional systems, which the source attributes mainly to water availability, and live fences of Gliricidia sepium, Leucaena leucocephala and similar species carry livestock through dry periods with high-quality fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Nyando District, Kenya, households in an agroforestry project typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, and many farmers reported selling fuel wood and timber from their trees to buy food during the drought [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].
agroforestry__drought__mixed_crop_livest.conditionality: The Kenyan household units are a single study of survey and farmer-interview evidence, and the link between agroforestry and perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5]. A Nigerian model study cited in a review (Onyekuru and Marchant), used as an income proxy, found no significant impact on agroforestry household net revenues under a simulated warmer, drier climate [ev_household_income_watts22_14]. The understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The Nyando units rest on income and coping strategies as proxies for drought impact, and the timber-sales finding is farmer-reported rather than measured [ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2]. Earlier work cited in a temperate alley-cropping study (Kowalchuk and Jong 1995) found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years, a high-income cropping result applied here by default [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. The Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].

agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.mechanism: On pastoral land the benefit runs through fodder and herd condition. Live fences of Gliricidia sepium, Leucaena leucocephala and similar species are used to feed livestock in the dry season and supply high-quality fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. In Colombia, a review citing Altieri and Nicholls 2013 reports that forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year (Murgueitio et al. 2011) [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During drought, understorey crop yield can be higher than in an open system, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].
agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.conditionality: The evidence base is thin and mostly second-hand: the silvopastoral units are earlier studies cited in a Spanish-language review and a CATIE edited volume, the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. Only the Latin American silvopastoral units come from pastoral rangeland systems; the live-fence review, the understorey statement, the Kenyan FMNR rating, the Honduran cropping result and the Nigerian income model are applied here by default [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. The understorey benefit reverses under normal rainfall, when tree shade could decrease understorey yields [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. The FMNR unit is a compiler rating, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. Against the benefit, earlier work cited in a temperate alley-cropping study (Kowalchuk and Jong 1995) found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of competition, a high-income cropping result, and a Nigerian model study cited in a review found no significant impact on agroforestry household net revenues under a simulated warmer, drier climate [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. The Colombian sources are upper-middle income, outside the LIC/LMIC target, and the Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].

agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.mechanism: In Cañas, Costa Rica, cattle on pasture with high tree density gained 2 to 5% more weight in the dry season than those on low-cover pasture, attributed partly to longer grazing and rumination under reduced heat stress [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Against this, earlier work cited in a temperate alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of tree–crop competition [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3].
agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.conditionality: The units point in opposite directions and neither measures drought losses in a pastoral system: the shelterbelt result is a temperate cropping finding applied to pastoral rangeland by default, and the Costa Rican result is dry-season liveweight gain [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Both are earlier findings cited second-hand, from high-income or temperate settings outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3].

agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.mechanism: In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the particularly severe El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves the micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates the impact of droughts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts].
agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.conditionality: Against those benefits, a model-based assessment cited in a tropical agroforestry review (Onyekuru and Marchant) found no significant impact on agroforestry household net revenues in Nigeria under a simulated climate 1◦C warmer with 7% less annual rainfall; it enters as an income proxy and is the no-benefit result that discounts the class [ev_household_income_watts22_14]. The Honduran observation repeats Welchez and Cherrett, cited in an ICRAF working paper, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. None of the units records a pastoral or rangeland farming system: the Honduran unit concerns crops and the others name no system, so they are applied to rangeland by default [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. All units are from lower-middle-income countries (Honduras, Kenya, Nigeria), inside the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.mechanism: In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25%, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are more drought-tolerant and give more stable forage volumes in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4].
agroforestry__drought__pastoral_rangelan.conditionality: All units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. The El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm, and the deep-root forage unit refers to the dry season without a size [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. The evidence comes from upper-middle-income Latin America, outside the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__drought__tree_perennial.mechanism: Under drought, trees in tree-crop systems have been found to protect the crop, to compete with it for water, and to make no difference. On the protective side, in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly positive for coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; reviews cite a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season (Lin) and low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]; and a review adds that under normal rainfall tree shade can lower understorey crop yields while during drought those yields can be higher than in an open system, even in intense shade [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. General agroforestry reports point the same way: in Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual system withstood the particularly severe 1997 drought while non-adopters suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]; live fences supply livestock fodder in the dry season, when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]; and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. On the competing side, reviews cite that under warmer, water-limited conditions competition between trees and cacao for scarce soil water can reduce soil moisture and cacao yields below those of open-sun farms (Blaser et al.), that drought caused greater water loss in cacao agroforests than in open-sun cacao because trees and cacao both transpire (Abdulai et al.), and that intercropping may compete for soil moisture during drought [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_9, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]; earlier work (Kowalchuk and Jong) cited in a German alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of competition [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. Between them sit no-effect findings: in a Ghanaian throughfall-exclusion experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on cocoa yield was not significant, so shade may not prevent the yield decline under drought [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian coffee study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in extreme climate shocks [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; on Bahia cocoa farms drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2]; and a model cited in a review (Onyekuru and Marchant) found no significant impact on Nigerian agroforestry household net revenues under a simulated warmer, drier climate [ev_household_income_watts22_14].
agroforestry__drought__tree_perennial.conditionality: The studies disagree, so the row states no direction. What separates the sides, as far as the evidence says, is whether the trees draw on the same scarce soil water as the crop: the losses are attributed to that competition and to combined tree and crop transpiration, while the gains come with a named companion tree (Gliricidia), a shade-management setting (canopy openness) or a drought year in which shade relieved the understorey [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_9, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. A second separator is what is measured: the Ghanaian experiment found the overall better performance of cocoa under shade can only partly compensate for the reduced yield during drought, so a higher yield under shade is not the same as protection from drought [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. Tree species, density and canopy management are therefore the design questions for drought-exposed tree-crop systems. The cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; the Ghanaian shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. Most units on both sides are second-hand readings in reviews, and only the evapotranspiration figure carries a size [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]. Only the cocoa and coffee units record a tree-perennial system; the Honduran, live-fence, FMNR, Nigerian, understorey and shelterbelt units record none and are applied here by default, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating rather than a measurement [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_household_income_watts22_14, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. The field units are from low-income Ethiopia, lower-middle-income Ghana and upper-middle-income Brazil [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2].

agroforestry__drought__tree_perennial__i.mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income tree-crop settings, trees in the system give a slight reduction in drought impact at best. In Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest, the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade trees strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, an ICRAF working paper citing Welchez and Cherrett 2002 reports that crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the particularly severe El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. The Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts].
agroforestry__drought__tree_perennial__i.conditionality: As many units find no benefit as find one, which is why the class is slight. In a Ghana rainwater-suppression experiment on cocoa, the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline and the better performance of cocoa under shade only partly compensated for it; the shade there came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. The same Ethiopian coffee study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in the extreme climate shocks [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2], and a Nigerian model study cited in a review found no significant impact on agroforestry household net revenues under a simulated warmer, drier climate [ev_household_income_watts22_14]. What separates gains from nulls is shade management (the Ethiopian gain appears at high canopy openness) and how severe the shock is [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. Only the cocoa and coffee units are measured in tree-crop systems; they are crop-specific and enter under the shaded perennial-crop scope ruling, while the Honduran, Kenyan and Nigerian units are applied to tree-crop systems by default [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. The FMNR unit is a compiler rating, not a measurement, and the Honduran point is an earlier finding cited second-hand [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].

agroforestry__drought_hazard.mechanism: Trees on farms slightly reduce the damage drought does to farm households. In two Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, a farmer said deep-rooted mango trees get water from deep down, others said trees do not dry up fast and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10]. Reviews report that under drought understorey crop yields could be higher than in an open system even in intense shade, that trees were the most important source of animal food and milk for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought (Chibinga et al. 2012), that live fences supply livestock fodder when pasture is scarce, and that agroforestry biomass production varied less over 4 years than conventional systems in semi-arid Brazil, attributed mainly to water availability (Martins et al. 2013) [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6]. In an eastern Canadian soybean intercrop, experimentally induced drought caused crop losses in the monocrop only (Nasielski et al. 2015) [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates drought impacts as reduced, its compiler judging that FMNR improves micro-climate and soil moisture and therefore mitigates the impact of droughts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts].
agroforestry__drought_hazard.conditionality: Effects are not uniform: the same review says tree shade could decrease understorey yields under normal rainfall, and the Senegal review reports no clear consensus on windbreaks in drought, some studies finding higher yields in drier years and others harm to rainfed crops [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. In Kenya the link between agroforestry and perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna, and one Kenyan unit states only that agroforestry has been proposed for resilience [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Few units give a size, so the class is slight. Most units are reviews repeating earlier studies or household perception, the Canadian trial is high-income evidence, and the Kenyan FMNR unit is a practitioner judgement on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The household and fodder evidence comes largely from lower-middle-income Kenya and low-income Zambia, inside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14].

agroforestry__frost__all.conditionality: The cell rests on microclimate evidence (night-time canopy temperature and radiation), a component of frost impact, rather than measured frost losses on farms [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_5]. Brazilian units (upper-middle income) and a review statement has no recorded country or income group; none is from an LIC/LMIC setting, and the transfer is classed adjacent [ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_5, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_3]. All three are reviews or authors citing earlier work, and none records a farming system, so the evidence is applied to each farming system by default [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_souza11_5].
