agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__heat_.conditionality: This is a background statement in a Kenyan livelihood-resilience study that cites earlier work (Lin 2007) rather than a measurement made in that study [ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3]. Microclimate buffering is used as a component proxy for heat stress, and the quote refers to shade trees generally without naming crops, livestock or farming systems [ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__heat_.mechanism: A poplar tree-based alley-cropping system in Germany had a 3.4°C lower temperature than sole wheat on hot summer days, and in Kenya shade trees are described as producing microclimates that buffer temperature fluctuations and can reduce evapotranspiration [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__heat_.conditionality: Both units are second-hand: a German unit (high income, temperate Europe) and a Kenyan introduction statement citing earlier work, so a high-income unit carries a large share of this row [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3]. The Kenyan statement is about shade trees in general rather than a silvoarable design, and both rest on temperature, a component of heat-stress impact [ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__produ.mechanism: Fertiliser trees raised food crop value in Malawi, alley cropping roughly doubled crop yield against controls in a sub-Saharan meta-analysis, and wheat yield rose by 6.8% under reduced heat load in Indian agri-silviculture [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_3, ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_3, ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6]. A systematic review reports positive yield impacts for soil-fertility replenishment practices where soil fertility is severely depleted, and in Ethiopia land productivity improved where nitrogen-fixing trees were incorporated into the farming system [ev_t6_yield_soilfert_castle21_2, ev_crop_yield_ieg20_1]. Fertilizer trees raise maize output: in Malawi, adopters had a 35% higher value of food crop production and 32% higher maize productivity than their counterfactual, and a review notes fertilizer tree species are widely documented to substantially increase maize yields compared with maize grown without fertilizer in Zambia and across Africa [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_lasco14_1]. In maize–Gliricidia trials run for 12-13 consecutive years in Malawi and Zambia, the intercrop gave the most stable yield at Makoka and more stable yields than fertilized maize at Msekera, and the intercrop with 50% of the recommended N and P fertilizer matched the yield of fully fertilized monoculture maize [ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_2]. Maize yields were more stable with Leucaena hedgerows than in monocrop, as also shown for alley cropping and fertilizer trees [ev_yield_stability_lasco14_1]. Across 333 paddock years in a global quantitative review, alleys reduced yield by 17.63% on average and only 69 responses showed increases; paddocks with spacings between alleys under 10 tree heights were predicted to lose yield, with a reduction of more than 25% under 2.5 tree heights, while at 15 tree heights the predicted paddock yield increase was 13% [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_6, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__produ.conditionality: The units pull both ways: a Mozambique PES tree-planting programme lowered crop value, water competition with Grevillea robusta delayed Kenyan maize, intercropped wheat, maize and soybean yielded less than monocultures in China, Indonesia and Brazil, and improved fallows were not significant in a Kenyan production-function estimate [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_2, ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_4, ev_crop_yield_santos25_5, ev_crop_yield_place05_6]. The magnitude range runs from a single-digit wheat gain to a more-than-900% crop biomass gain under water stress in a Sahelian shrub intercrop, so it does not describe a typical effect [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1]. In southern Malawi a Tephrosia vogelii relay intercrop, which produces leafy residues but no grain, gave the same quantity of maize grain as monoculture maize fertilised in the same way, so no yield gain [ev_crop_yield_snapp10_1]. Gains are not universal: Malawian non-adopters would have lost food crop value had they adopted fertilizer trees, at Msekera fertilized monoculture maize out-yielded the maize–Gliricidia intercrop, and some stability models there ranked unfertilized control maize as more stable than the intercrop [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_3]. The Malawi estimates come from an ICRAF working paper evaluating an ICRAF-promoted technology, and the Gliricidia trials compare against fertilized maize rather than farmer practice [ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1]. Alley spacing separates the review's own losses from its gains: narrow spacings lose yield and the largest spacings gain [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8]. The tropical gains above come mainly from fertiliser-tree and Gliricidia systems on depleted African soils, whereas the review's alley systems exclude intercropping where trees and crops compete directly. The global review's main text gives no country or income-group breakdown, so its losses cannot be placed against the LIC/LMIC target, and its alley group includes pasture alleys and hedges [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_6].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__rural.mechanism: In western Kenya, returns to labour from improved fallows were 33 percent higher than from no-input continuous maize, about 87.5% of Lower Nyando farmers who had their trees for four years reported income improvements, and a Mozambique PES tree-planting programme significantly raised cash income per capita [ev_economic_return_place05_3, ev_t6_income_timebenefit_castle21_6, ev_household_income_castle21s_6]. In Ethiopia, market-oriented agroforestry with Acacia decurrens is credited with income, employment and reduced poverty in supported microwatersheds [ev_household_income_ieg20_3]. Fertilizer trees limit financial risk in drought years: where a crop fails, farmers using inorganic fertilizer lose the US$164 spent on the input, against US$90 for farmers who planted fertilizer trees [ev_economic_return_chaudhury11_1]. In southern Malawi, under higher fertiliser prices the value-cost ratio of a Tephrosia vogelii relay intercrop with maize stayed above 4.0, which the authors call a profitable scenario, while the higher prices pulled monoculture maize down to 2.5 or less [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__rural.conditionality: Several effects did not reach significance or reversed: Zambian improved fallows raised maize income but not total crop income, Kenyan improved fallows changed liquid assets positively but not significantly, and crop–fruit tree intercropping in China lowered gross income [ev_household_income_castle21s_4, ev_household_income_castle21s_5, ev_household_income_castle21s_2]. The Ethiopian unit is an evaluation lesson rather than a measured effect [ev_household_income_ieg20_3]. The Zambian figures are an earlier study cited in an ICRAF working paper and compare losses on crop failure rather than incomes [ev_economic_return_chaudhury11_1]. The Malawian value-cost ratio is a fertiliser-price scenario on on-farm trial data, not measured household income [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.mechanism: The direction comes mainly from a Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi. Water use efficiency was higher in the tree systems in every season, for example 1.97 against 0.15 g of biomass per kg of water for gliricidia + maize against sole maize in 1998/99, and 2.41 against 0.87 for gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea against maize + pigeonpea in 1999/00 [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. Available water content tended to be greater in the gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase, which the authors attribute to increased infiltration from improved soil structure and reduced soil evaporation under greater ground cover [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10], and in the second season's May that system held much more water than all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8]. A German alley-cropping trial in a drought year adds that soil water content remained lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. The same Malawi trial also records harm: the lower available soil water at the beginning of the cropping season in the tree-based systems suggests the trees continued to deplete moisture during the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2], the March-to-August decline was most pronounced in the tree-based systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3], water content was slightly lower under gliricidia + maize in the dry season when the trees were left unpruned [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5], and in the first season's May water content under gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea was lower than in all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4]. Other measurements found no difference: a generally comparable distribution of water in the profile [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1], and no significant treatment effects in the second season, the second season's October, or December and January of the third season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]. The authors conclude that gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season does not provoke undue competition for water with associated crops [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.conditionality: The positive direction leans on the water use efficiency figures, which are total above-ground biomass of trees and crops together per unit of seasonal water use, not grain per unit of water [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1]. Gliricidia biomass lifts the tree-system values, and the authors caution that soil evaporation and water-table uptake were not measured, so the gap is probably overstated; these units count for water stress only and are held out of the production gap because they do not measure crop yield. Timing and depth set the limits: the trees deplete dry-season and subsoil water, so crops may start the season with less, while recharge-season water favours the tree plots [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10]. The result holds for gliricidia pruned before and during the crop season and left unpruned after harvest; unpruned or denser tree rows are not covered [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5]. Nearly all the evidence comes from one research-station trial in southern Malawi. The German trial counts little: a temperate high-income site whose differences were not significant at all positions, measuring surface soil only [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.mechanism: Under waterlogging in Punjab, India, agroforestry systems had higher evapotranspiration than sole crops, removing excess water from the soil and creating a better soil environment for plant growth [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.conditionality: This is one Indian study (lower-middle income, within the LIC/LMIC target) reported second-hand in a review [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.mechanism: Under waterlogging in Punjab, India, agroforestry systems had higher evapotranspiration than sole crops, removing excess water from the soil and creating a better soil environment for plant growth [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__water.conditionality: This is one Indian study (lower-middle income, within the LIC/LMIC target) reported second-hand in a review [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9]. All units are from irrigated cropping systems [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9].

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__wind_.mechanism: The only evidence is a background statement in a Kenyan livelihood-resilience study that trees have the ability to buffer crops from storms, citing earlier work [ev_t3_wind_buffer_quandt17_4].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__wind_.conditionality: It is not a measurement made in that study, refers to crops rather than livestock or structures, and gives no tree arrangement, species or storm intensity [ev_t3_wind_buffer_quandt17_4]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__wind_.mechanism: The only evidence is a background statement in a Kenyan livelihood-resilience study that trees have the ability to buffer crops from storms, citing earlier work [ev_t3_wind_buffer_quandt17_4].
agroforestry__planted_silvoarable__wind_.conditionality: It is not a measurement made in that study, refers to crops rather than livestock or structures, and gives no tree arrangement, species or storm intensity [ev_t3_wind_buffer_quandt17_4]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__production_gap.mechanism: The production evidence splits by sub-practice. Gains are consistent in regeneration-based farmland and in the cross-family syntheses, while planted silvoarable, silvopastoral, boundary and shaded perennial (coffee and cocoa) systems record both gains and losses. Meta-analyses report higher crop yield under agroforestry than controls in sub-Saharan Africa and higher soil nitrogen stocks than crop monocultures in the humid tropics, with soil nitrogen used here as a component of the production gap [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. A meta-analysis cited in Arslan et al. (Branca et al.) associates agroforestry techniques with a 69% increase in cereal yields across the studies it consulted [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. In the Sahel, millet yields are reported to double or triple under Faidherbia albida and yields were higher where intensive FMNR is practised, and tree shade in pastures is associated with gains in milk production and weight gain [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_8, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_14, ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns yielded 23-26% more grain than open-field wheat in the normal seasons of 2013 and 2014, and up to 85% more in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low; available N close to the crowns was 35-55% larger than under sole wheat [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_1]. WOCAT practitioner ratings for FMNR in Kenya and assisted natural regeneration in Burkina Faso record higher crop and fodder production, the Kenyan compiler adding that well-managed FMNR land gives more and better-quality fodder than unmanaged land [ev_crop_yield_wocat_507_2019_crop_production, ev_crop_yield_wocat_1358_2017_crop_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_507_2019_fodder_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_1358_2017_fodder_production]. Lower yield variability under more diverse shade is cited as a sign of greater yield resistance to shocks in shaded systems, and Kenyan agroforestry-project farmers in Lower Nyando raised farm productivity against a control group [ev_crop_yield_morel24_4, ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. Fertilizer trees raise maize output: in Malawi, adopters had a 35% higher value of food crop production and 32% higher maize productivity than their counterfactual, and a review notes fertilizer tree species are widely documented to substantially increase maize yields compared with maize grown without fertilizer in Zambia and across Africa [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_lasco14_1]. In maize–Gliricidia trials run for 12-13 consecutive years in Malawi and Zambia, the intercrop gave the most stable yield at Makoka and more stable yields than fertilized maize at Msekera, and the intercrop with 50% of the recommended N and P fertilizer matched the yield of fully fertilized monoculture maize [ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_2]. Maize yields were more stable with Leucaena hedgerows than in monocrop, as also shown for alley cropping and fertilizer trees [ev_yield_stability_lasco14_1]. In Maradi, Niger, millet yields rose by 120 to 209 kg/ha where FMNR was older than 6 years, with smaller increases for younger FMNR, and FMNR is estimated to have raised yields by an average of 100 kg/ha over 5 million hectares [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3]. In Lempira, Honduras, the Quesungual system raised maize yields from 1.9 to 3.2 tonnes per hectare and bean yields from 0.8 to 2.0 tonnes per hectare, and its crops withstood the severe 1997 drought that caused losses for non-adopters [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_2, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, tuber yield is improved (+0.40 to +1.67 t ha-1) and legumes are less affected than cereals, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. A meta-analysis of Chinese farmland shelterbelts found crop yield 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]. In subarctic Ontario, a site lined by willow windbreaks produced about 300 g/m2 of bean pods against about 60 g/m2 at an open site, and potato tuber yield was 33% greater (3200 versus 2400 g/m2) [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. In Colombian intensive silvopasture, milk production was 32.1% higher than with the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Intensive silvopasture raises stocking rates up to four times above extensive grazing and with them meat and milk output per hectare [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1]. In Colombia, a Leucaena-based silvopastoral system raised stocking to 4.3 cows ha-1 while eliminating chemical fertiliser [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25%, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are more drought-tolerant and give more stable forage volumes in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During El Niño events, milk production fell by 2.2% in silvopastoral systems against 4.9% in conventional systems [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover and above 15% in silvopasture compared with full sun, and dry-season weight gains were 2 to 5% higher on high tree-density pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. In shaded coffee and cocoa, a coffee meta-analysis found agroforestry reduced the odds of climate-related yield loss (OR = 0.69) and a cocoa meta-analysis found total system yields about ten times higher than in monocultures [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_2].
agroforestry__production_gap.conditionality: The sub-practices disagree, so the roll-up states conflicting evidence rather than a strong gain. On the gain side, regeneration-based farmland (Faidherbia albida and Piliostigma reticulatum parklands, FMNR in Niger and Ghana, the Quesungual system) and the cross-family meta-analyses and assessments show higher yields or soil nitrogen [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_9, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_15, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_talensi21_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1, ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4]. On the conflicting side, shaded perennial systems pair those system-level gains with main-crop losses: cocoa yields 25% lower than in monocultures, coffee and cocoa yield per hectare 26% lower than conventional systems, and coffee yields declining under >60% shade, while shade did not prevent the drought-induced cocoa yield decline in a Ghanaian experiment [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1, ev_crop_yield_patil25_3, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the separator there is whether the by-crops are counted and how dense the shade is, and the units are crop-specific to coffee, cocoa and coconut. Planted silvoarable systems pair fertilizer-tree and Gliricidia gains with tree–crop competition losses; silvopasture pairs Latin American milk and stocking gains with a global review's losses under dispersed trees; and boundary planting pairs higher yields within sheltered farmland with losses at shelterbelt edges and in windbreak paddocks [ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_2, ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14, ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1]. The separator, in the sources' own terms, is spacing, tree density, tree age and distance from the tree line: alley spacings under 10 TH were predicted to reduce yields, pasture yield fell as tree density rose and under the oldest trees, livestock yield fell with more trees and older trees, and yield losses were reported up to 10 m from hedges in the rainy season and in shelterbelt edge zones [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_10, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_12, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_15, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_16, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]. The global review's main text gives no country or income-group breakdown, so its losses cannot be placed against the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1]. The evidence pulls both ways: tree–crop competition for water delayed Kenyan maize and could cause crop failure, intercropped wheat in China and soybean in Brazil yielded less than monocultures, groundnut and millet yields fell under Cordyla pinnata in Senegal, and excess shade can reduce pasture productivity [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_crop_yield_santos25_5, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_11, ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14]. The pooled magnitude combines a crop-yield response ratio with a soil-nitrogen response ratio, and a systematic review's pooled crop-yield effect across agroforestry interventions had a confidence interval spanning zero [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_1]. The WOCAT units are compiler judgements on documented technology sheets, not yield measurements [ev_crop_yield_wocat_507_2019_crop_production, ev_crop_yield_wocat_1358_2017_crop_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_507_2019_fodder_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_1358_2017_fodder_production]. The Lower Nyando productivity gain had large standard errors and was not significant, earlier work cited in a temperate alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years, and the yield-variability finding is a cited statement [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4]. Gains are not universal: Malawian non-adopters would have lost food crop value had they adopted fertilizer trees, at Msekera fertilized monoculture maize out-yielded the maize–Gliricidia intercrop, and some stability models there ranked unfertilized control maize as more stable than the intercrop [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_3]. The Malawi estimates come from an ICRAF working paper evaluating an ICRAF-promoted technology, and the Gliricidia trials compare against fertilized maize rather than farmer practice [ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1]. Cereals often lose: in Maradi, FMNR did not significantly increase grain yields, the income gain being attributed to crop diversification instead, and under parkland trees cereal grain yield ranged from a loss of 0.54 t ha-1 under Balanites aegyptiaca to a gain of 0.24 t ha-1 under F. albida, with reductions attributed to competition for light, nutrients and water [ev_crop_yield_haglund11_1, ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1]. The Niger yield figures are earlier estimates cited in a grey-literature review, and the Honduran yields are before-and-after case-study figures for a slash-and-mulch system [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1]. Next to the trees the effect reverses: crop yield in shelterbelt edge zones fell by an average of 20.47% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]. In the West African Sahel, live fences and fodder banks reduced yields in the first year, which recovered in the second [ev_crop_yield_lasco14_2]. Tree density matters: dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. The Latin American livestock units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The Costa Rican livestock units are high-income evidence [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. A global quantitative review against treeless controls found average losses for windbreaks, alleys and dispersed trees: windbreak paddocks −8.3%, alleys −17.63%, pasture under dispersed trees −20.8% and livestock there −18.6%, with gains only at wide spacings (+13% at 15 tree heights between alleys, +8.04% across a windbreak paddock 20 tree heights wide) [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_6, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_9, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5]. The cited 69% cereal-yield figure reaches this row second-hand through Arslan et al.: the citing text does not describe the agroforestry techniques further and reports no significance [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. Of the newer primary studies, regeneration-based farmland again holds the stronger result: The Ethiopian drought-year gain stays separate from the normal-season gain; at the same site soil total N did not differ significantly under and outside the canopy at the end of the 2013 season despite the larger available N near the crowns, and the yield benefit of canopy cooling is modelled and appeared only with applied N [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_2, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. The Ontario windbreak gain is high-income boreal evidence from a single windbreak-lined site against a single open site, with plots irrigated from ditches, so it does not test the water competition near trees that drives the dry-year losses [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. In southern Malawi a Tephrosia vogelii relay intercrop, which produces leafy residues but no grain, gave the same quantity of maize grain as monoculture maize fertilised in the same way, so no yield gain [ev_crop_yield_snapp10_1].

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: Parkland trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, crucial in the dry season and during drought, and in Senegal access to cool zones under trees reduces livestock heat stress and so raises animal productivity [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22]. Under parkland trees, tuber yield is improved (+0.40 to +1.67 t ha-1) and legumes are less affected by tree cover [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1].
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: Cereals lose out: grain yield ranged from a loss of 0.54 t ha-1 under Balanites aegyptiaca to a gain of 0.24 t ha-1 under F. albida, with reductions attributed to competition for light, nutrients and water, so the net effect depends on which crops dominate [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1]. All units are reviews citing earlier studies from the Sahel and Senegal, and the fodder and livestock gains are stated without a size [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22].

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: In the Brazilian semi-arid, tree leaves added nitrogen in a cactus pear and buffel grass association, with potential to cut fertiliser cost, and a silvopastoral system gave higher mean bodyweight gain per animal than the monoculture [ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7, ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers in an agroforestry project improved farm productivity on average against a control group [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1].
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: The Kenyan productivity gain had large standard errors and was not significant, and soil nitrogen is a component rather than a yield measure [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. The Brazilian units are cited secondary results from an upper-middle-income country, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target, while the Kenyan unit is lower-middle income [ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7, ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1].

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: In rangeland and pasture systems trees raise livestock output through forage, shade and higher stocking. In the Senegalese Ferlo, herbaceous biomass under Acacia tortilis and Balanites aegyptiaca canopies was 2 to 5 times that of treeless areas, and tree leaves, fruit and pods make up about 40 per cent of cattle and 80 per cent of small-ruminant diets late in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. In Latin American silvopasture, tree shade is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]; milk was 32.1% higher in intensive silvopasture than with the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Stocking rises up to four times above extensive grazing, reaching 4.3 cows ha-1 in a Colombian Leucaena system that eliminated chemical fertiliser [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1, ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. Milk rose 29% on high tree-density pasture against low tree cover and above 15% in silvopasture against full sun, with dry-season weight gains 2 to 5% higher [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Under drought, forage held constant in a Colombian silvopastoral system while grass-monoculture biomass fell to 25 %, deep-rooted trees give steadier dry-season forage, cattle are better fed in critical drought periods, milk fell by 2.2% against 4.9% in conventional systems during El Niño events, and at El Hatico milk still rose 10% in 2009, the driest year in decades (440 mm) [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2, ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4].
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: The row carries a harm signal tied to tree density: dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture (1110 trees/ha) gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field, while the low-density stand (407 trees/ha) gave 16.6 L [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. Every unit is an earlier study read second-hand through a FAO country assessment, Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume, and none is a pastoral-system experiment run by the citing authors [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3]. The Senegalese diet shares describe how much of the ration comes from trees, not a measured production change [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. Most of the Latin American evidence is intensive silvopasture with Leucaena shrubs in upper-middle-income Colombia, and the Costa Rican units are high-income; milk gains attributed to heat relief also reflect extra foliage and fruit [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1]. The El Hatico result is a single farm compared year on year, and the Colombian drought-forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1].

agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.mechanism: In tree-crop systems, shade trees have been found to raise output, to lower the main-crop yield, and to make no difference. On the gain side, a global coffee meta-analysis found agroforestry reduced the odds of climate-related yield loss (OR = 0.69) and improved continuous outcomes such as yield, bean size and quality (SMD = +0.42) [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1, ev_crop_yield_patil25_2]; in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest, leguminous shade trees and low canopy openness generally benefited yields, and leguminous shade strongly raised yields at high canopy openness in the shock years [ev_crop_yield_morel24_3, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; a cocoa meta-analysis found total system yields about ten times higher than monocultures, and a review citing Pérez-Neira et al. reports total agroforestry production three times that of monocultures [ev_crop_yield_niether20_2, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_9]; moderate shade gave coffee yields similar to or 3% higher than full sun (Pinoargote et al. 2016) [ev_crop_yield_villa20_4]; shaded coffee in Paraná, Brazil yielded up to 101.99 kg/ha in its second year where the unshaded control yielded zero [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1]; nitrogen fixed in coffee under Erythrina poeppigiana or Inga edulis is around 100 kg ha-1 (Leblanc et al. 2007) [ev_soil_nitrogen_villa20_12]; and shade trees are cited as reducing the biennial swing in coffee yields and, in other studies, lowering yield variability under more diverse shade [ev_yield_stability_montagnini15_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4]. On the loss side, the same cocoa meta-analysis found cocoa yields 25% lower than in monocultures, a shaded coffee and cocoa meta-analysis found productivity per hectare 26% lower than conventional systems, and reviews cite cocoa productivity 41% higher in monocultures (Armengot et al. 2016), coffee yield 30% lower once shade was established (Siles et al.), and coffee fruit production 41% lower under 40 to 60% Erythrina shade than under at most 20% cover (Estivariz 1997) [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_6, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11, ev_crop_yield_villa20_1]. Coffee yields declined under >60% shade from reduced light and humidity-linked disease, high cocoa yield (> 1.5 t/ha) is only possible below 100-150 t C/ha of carbon storage, and shade trees can harm cocoa under severe drought, depending on species (Abdulai et al. 2018), as can tree–cacao water competition (Blaser et al. 2018) [ev_crop_yield_patil25_3, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_6, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_3, ev_crop_yield_watts22_8]. A further set of studies finds no difference: no yield effect of shade in a coffee case study, in shaded coffee under 30% cover in Costa Rica (Cerda et al. 2016) or in fruiting nodes of young shaded coffee (Angrand et al. 2004); no relation between shade and cocoa drought loss in Bahia or coffee hurricane loss in Chiapas; shade not preventing the drought yield decline in a Ghana cocoa experiment or showing a benefit in Ethiopia's extreme shock; and no soil nitrogen difference across cocoa systems [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_2, ev_crop_yield_villa20_3, ev_crop_yield_villa20_2, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_niether20_1].
agroforestry__production_gap__farming_sy.conditionality: Studies disagree, and what separates the sides is largely what is counted and how much shade there is. Counting the main crop alone, cocoa and coffee yields are usually lower under shade; counting the whole system, including timber, fruit and other by-crops, output is higher — the same cocoa meta-analysis reports both, as does the review citing total production [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_2, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_9]. Revenue can offset the yield gap: the review reporting cocoa 41% higher in monocultures adds that agroforestry revenues compensate economically for the difference [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_6]. Shade level is the second separator: 30 to 60% shade gave the most favourable coffee results and yields declined above 60%, moderate shade matched full sun, and the 41% coffee fruit loss came at 40 to 60% Erythrina cover against at most 20% [ev_crop_yield_patil25_3, ev_crop_yield_villa20_4, ev_crop_yield_villa20_1]; but the coffee meta-analysis found that no moderator, shade density included, explained a statistically significant share of the variance [ev_crop_yield_patil25_9]. Shade-tree species, density and canopy openness are therefore the design questions, and management intensity can matter more than shade itself [ev_crop_yield_villa20_3, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]. Under shocks the evidence leans to no shade effect either way [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. Many units are earlier studies repeated in Portuguese-, Spanish- or French-language reviews and a CATIE edited volume; the coffee, cocoa and shaded coffee-and-cocoa meta-analyses are the main syntheses [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1]. The nitrogen units are soil-fertility components, not yield measures, and the Paraná result depends on tree species and development [ev_soil_nitrogen_villa20_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1]. All units are crop-specific to coffee or cocoa except the system-production and yield-variability statements; located evidence spans low-income Ethiopia, lower-middle-income Ghana, upper-middle-income Brazil and Mexico and high-income Costa Rica, so the transfer to LIC/LMIC tree-crop systems is adjacent [ev_crop_yield_morel24_3, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6, ev_crop_yield_villa20_3].

agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.mechanism: In high-income settings, agroforestry has been found both to raise and to lower output. Gains: in subarctic Ontario, a site lined by willow windbreaks produced about 300 g/m2 of bean pods against about 60 g/m2 at an open site, and potato tuber yield was 33% greater (3200 versus 2400 g/m2) [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]; cited studies from Cañas, Costa Rica found milk production more than 15% higher for cows grazing silvopasture than in full sun and dry-season weight gains 2 to 5% higher on high tree-density pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]; and a cited Costa Rican study found moderate shade gave coffee yields similar to, or 3% higher than, full sun [ev_crop_yield_villa20_4]. Losses: a cited Costa Rican experiment recorded a 30% coffee yield reduction in the shaded system against coffee monoculture [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11], and earlier work cited in a temperate alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of tree–crop competition [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3].
agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.conditionality: What separates the sides is the system and the competition for resources. The gains are livestock under tree cover and windbreak-sheltered vegetables in Ontario, where the plots were irrigated from ditches, whereas the losses are crops competing with trees: shelterbelt-edge cropping in dry years and established shade over coffee [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11]. In Costa Rican coffee several units find no difference: a case study recorded no negative yield effect of shade, systems under 30 % shade cover did not differ in yield from full sun with management intensity driving yield instead, and young shaded coffee did not differ in fruiting nodes [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_2, ev_crop_yield_villa20_3, ev_crop_yield_villa20_2]. All units are from high-income settings outside the LIC/LMIC target; most are earlier findings read second-hand through reviews, while the Ontario result was measured directly but at a single windbreak-lined site against a single open site [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_crop_yield_villa20_3, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1]. The coffee units are crop-specific [ev_crop_yield_villa20_4, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11].

agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.mechanism: In upper-middle-income settings, agroforestry moderately narrows the production gap on balance, mainly through livestock and sheltered-crop gains, though intercropped crops can lose output. Gains: wheat and barley intercropped 2.5 m from trees in Iran out-yielded monocultures by 35% and 39% [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_2]; a meta-analysis of Chinese farmland shelterbelts found crop yield 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland, alongside microclimatic improvements [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]; tree leaves added about 40 kg ha-1 of nitrogen in a Brazilian cactus pear and buffel grass system [ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]; and on the livestock side, Brazilian silvopasture gave higher daily bodyweight gain per animal, Colombian intensive silvopasture gave 32.1% more milk than the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, stocking reached 4.3 cows ha-1 while chemical fertiliser was eliminated, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Under drought, forage in a Colombian silvopastoral system stayed constant while grass monoculture biomass fell to 25%, deep-rooted trees give more stable dry-season forage, milk fell by 2.2% against 4.9% in conventional systems during El Niño events, and at El Hatico milk still rose 10% in 2009, the driest year in decades at 440 mm [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Losses: intercropped wheat in China and maize in Indonesia yielded significantly less than monocultures, and Brazilian soybean gave about 500 and 700 kg ha-1 against about 3000 and 2700 kg ha-1 in monoculture, attributed to lower radiation [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_4, ev_crop_yield_santos25_5]; crop yield in shelterbelt edge zones fell by an average of 20.47% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]; and dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. In perennial crops, shaded coffee in Paraná, Brazil yielded up to 101.99 kg/ha in its second year where the unshaded monoculture control yielded zero [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1], and a coconut review reports, second-hand, increased nut yields when pasture, black pepper and coffee were intercropped with coconut [ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1].
agroforestry__production_gap__income_gro.conditionality: The benefit outweighs the losses, but the losses are real: measured harm appears in several sources, and what separates the gains from the losses is visible in the evidence. Production system: the livestock and silvopasture units are almost all gains, while the losses are concentrated in crops intercropped with trees, where shading and competition reduce the crop [ev_crop_yield_santos25_5, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3]. Distance and density: within one Chinese meta-analysis, yield rose across sheltered farmland but fell in the edge zone next to the trees, and the two figures are not to be netted [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]; in Colombia, dense Acacia lowered milk per cow while sparser planting raised it [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. Management: the soybean loss is attributed to radiation, which the authors tie to pruning and management of the system [ev_crop_yield_santos25_5]. For a Task Team Leader, the actionable distinctions are system type, tree spacing and density, and canopy management. On evidence quality, most units on both sides are earlier results cited in Portuguese- or Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the shelterbelt meta-analysis is the main primary synthesis and supplies one figure on each side [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_2, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]. The nitrogen unit is a soil-fertility component rather than a yield measure [ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7], and the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year, with the Colombian forage result likely describing the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. Under shocks the perennial-crop evidence finds no shade effect either way: cocoa yield loss in the Bahian drought was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover, and Mexican coffee farms lost 18 to 40% of their harvest after a hurricane regardless of vegetation management [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. The Paraná coffee result depends on tree species and development, and the coffee and coconut units are crop-specific [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.mechanism: The compiler of the Burkina Faso WOCAT sheet on assisted natural regeneration of degraded land judged that the technology copes well with local rainstorm [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1358_2017_local_rainstorm].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.conditionality: The cell rests on a single practitioner judgement from a documented technology sheet in low-income Burkina Faso, not measured damage, and the rating itself describes good coping [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1358_2017_local_rainstorm].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.mechanism: Fire is named among the factors behind the lack of regeneration in ageing agroforestry parklands, alongside climate change, grazing, removal of spontaneous shoots and the forest code [ev_fire_hazard_seghieri19_16]. The compiler of the Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet judged that the technology copes not well with forest fire or land fire [ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_forest_fire, ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_land_fire].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.conditionality: Fire is among several listed threats and its separate effect is not measured; the parkland unit is from lower-middle-income Senegal, within the LIC/LMIC target, and concerns long-term parkland persistence [ev_fire_hazard_seghieri19_16]. The Kenyan coping ratings are practitioner judgements from the same technology sheet, not measured damage [ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_forest_fire, ev_asset_fire_wocat_507_2019_land_fire].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.mechanism: WOCAT compilers judged assisted natural regeneration of degraded land in Burkina Faso to cope well with general river flood, and FMNR in Kenya to cope moderately with flash flood [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1358_2017_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_507_2019_flash_flood].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.conditionality: Both units are practitioner judgements on documented technology sheets, not measured damage, from regeneration practices in low-income Burkina Faso and lower-middle-income Kenya [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1358_2017_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_507_2019_flash_flood].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.mechanism: The compiler of the Burkina Faso WOCAT sheet on assisted natural regeneration of degraded land judged that the technology copes well with local windstorm [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__ass.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is a single practitioner rating on a technology sheet from low-income Burkina Faso, about local windstorms rather than cyclones, with no measured damage, so it does not show the regenerated trees are undamaged [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1358_2017_local_windstorm]. A second independent source or one measured finding of wind damage to regenerated trees would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__bio.mechanism: The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates gains in animal, habitat and plant diversity, its compiler noting that many animal species find safe habitats in new FMNR sites, that regenerated sites offer more habitats in trees and soil than degraded sites, and that indigenous tree populations and density increase [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_plant_diversity]. In Niger's Maradi region, FMNR adoption appears to raise tree diversity by between one and three species per farm and tree density by between 12 and 16 trees per hectare compared with matched non-adopters [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__bio.conditionality: The Kenyan units come from a WOCAT technology sheet for FMNR in lower-middle-income Kenya and are compiler judgements comparing regenerated with degraded sites, not species surveys [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_plant_diversity]. The Niger result is a matched comparison of adopters with non-adopters that counts tree species on farms, not wider biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__car.mechanism: In Sudano-Sahelian cropland, shrubs and trees on agricultural fields had an overall positive but variable effect on soil total carbon (+ 20 to 75%), and a cited meta-analysis reports that soil under Faidherbia albida canopy holds on average 46 per cent more organic carbon than outside it [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. The externally audited Humbo FMNR project in Ethiopia reports CO2 sequestered since 2007 [ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. WOCAT practitioner ratings add that FMNR in Kenya sequesters carbon in biomass through increased tree cover and raises soil organic matter, and the Burkina Faso assisted natural regeneration sheet rates a large gain in soil organic matter [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_507_2019_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_1358_2017_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__car.conditionality: Two literature units measure soil carbon under trees (a component of sequestration), and the Humbo figure is a project total from a World Vision self-evaluation with no per-hectare or per-year denominator [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. The literature is from semi-arid West Africa and Ethiopia (low- and lower-middle-income countries) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. The WOCAT units are compiler judgements on documented technology sheets, not measured stocks or rates [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_1358_2017_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C]. Measured directly on Ethiopian wheat farms, soil organic C did not differ significantly under and outside the Faidherbia albida canopy at the end of the 2013 cropping season, so the cited 46 per cent canopy gain was not reproduced at that site; this null lowers the agreement rather than the class [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__cat.mechanism: A review reports that Ilstedt et al., combining canopy interception and transpiration data of trees with their effects on water infiltration, derived an optimal intermediate tree density for parklands from a groundwater-recharge perspective; recharge is read here as a component of catchment water yield [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vannoordwijk21_6].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__cat.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state an effect for this cell: it is one modelling result read second-hand, with no measured finding and no country, and it points to an intermediate optimum rather than more trees always raising recharge [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vannoordwijk21_6]. A second independent source or one measured finding on water yield or recharge under regenerated farmland trees would let the cell state a class.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__cos.mechanism: The Regreening Africa cost-efficiency analysis reports that adopting land restoration practices in Ghana, where the arm was mainly FMNR, cost $66 per household, a programme cost per adopting household [ev_project_cost_crs23_1].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__cos.conditionality: This is a programme expenditure per adopting household for one lower-middle-income country arm of one programme, so it does not pool with other sources [ev_project_cost_crs23_1]. The same quote notes FMNR in Ghana cost less per household than tree-planting agroforestry in Rwanda [ev_project_cost_crs23_1].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__est.mechanism: The Regreening Africa cost-efficiency analysis reports that adopting land restoration practices in Ghana, where the arm was mainly FMNR, cost $66 per household, a programme cost per adopting household [ev_project_cost_crs23_1].

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__fir.mechanism: The only evidence is the compiler of the Kenyan WOCAT sheet on Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR), who comments that tree cover can increase the risk of major wildfires and advises fire breaks for larger FMNR sites [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk].
agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__fir.conditionality: The cell rests on a single practitioner judgement from a documented technology sheet in lower-middle-income Kenya, not a measured change in fire occurrence or damage [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__regeneration_farmland__flo.mechanism: The only evidence is the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR), who states that it also mitigates the impact of annual floods on crops and settlements [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_507_2019_flood_impacts].
