All units are crop-specific (cocoa or coffee) and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop. The Ghana shade came from artificial shade nets, not shade trees, so it has no below-ground competition and its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. The review units are second-hand readings of earlier studies, and only the evapotranspiration figure carries a size [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11, ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_9, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]. The field units are from upper-middle-income Brazil, low-income Ethiopia and lower-middle-income Ghana; the review units record no country [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood__a.mechanism: The only evidence is a review's second-hand statement that in Mesoamerica coffee-based agroforestry can help prevent flood occurrences, reducing the adverse impact of extreme rainfall events [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood__a.conditionality: This single unit is crop-specific (coffee) and enters because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; it records no country or income group and no measured flood loss [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood__t.mechanism: The only evidence is a review's second-hand statement that in Mesoamerica coffee-based agroforestry can help prevent flood occurrences, reducing the adverse impact of extreme rainfall events [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood__t.conditionality: This single unit is crop-specific (coffee) and enters because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; it records no country or income group and no measured flood loss [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood_ha.mechanism: A review reports, second-hand, that coffee-based agroforestry in Mesoamerica can regulate ecological services including preventing flood occurrences, helping reduce the adverse impact of extreme rainfall events [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__flood_ha.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a class: it is a single second-hand review sentence with no effect size, no country or income group, and a general claim about what coffee agroforestry can do rather than a measured flood outcome [ev_flood_hazard_dobhal24_12]. A further independent source or a measured finding for shaded perennial systems is what is missing.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.mechanism: Shade over cocoa and coffee lowers the temperature the crop experiences. A pantropical synthesis of cocoa studies found that the shade-tree canopy reduces solar radiation, so mean temperature stays lower and daily maximum and minimum temperatures are buffered compared with monocultures [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. A coffee review cites shade trees reducing canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C, mitigating heat stress (Lin et al. 2008; Meylan et al. 2017), and the IPCC notes, citing Ovalle-Rivera et al. 2015 and Schroth et al. 2015, that shade trees can ameliorate the rising stand temperatures that will significantly affect arabica coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. Measured on plots, shade cut maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C in Costa Rican coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.conditionality: The IPCC sentence that credits shade trees adds that the opposite can also be true, so the cooling is not guaranteed [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. Every unit points to cooling, but the evidence does not say how much that cuts crop losses. All units report temperature, a component of heat-stress impact, not measured crop heat-stress losses, and none is at severe or extreme heat. All are crop-specific (cocoa or coffee) and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop. The Costa Rican measurement is recorded as high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]; and the review and IPCC statements are second-hand readings of earlier studies [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.mechanism: Shade over cocoa and coffee lowers the temperature the crop experiences. A pantropical synthesis of cocoa studies found that the shade-tree canopy reduces solar radiation, so mean temperature stays lower and daily maximum and minimum temperatures are buffered compared with monocultures [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. A review cites shade trees reducing canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C, mitigating heat stress, and the IPCC notes that shade trees can ameliorate the rising stand temperatures that will significantly affect arabica coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. Measured on plots, shade cut maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C in Costa Rican coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.conditionality: The IPCC sentence that credits shade trees adds that the opposite can also be true, so the cooling is not guaranteed [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. All units report temperature, a component of heat-stress impact, not measured crop heat-stress losses, and none is at severe or extreme heat. All are crop-specific (cocoa or coffee) and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop. The Costa Rican measurement is recorded as high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]; and the review and IPCC statements are second-hand readings of earlier studies [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.mechanism: Shade trees over coffee and cocoa lower the temperature the crop experiences. A pan-tropical meta-analysis found that the shade-tree canopy reduces solar radiation, so mean temperature stays lower and daily maxima and minima are buffered in cocoa agroforestry against full-sun monocultures [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1], and a coffee review reports, citing Lin et al. 2008 and Meylan et al. 2017, that shade trees reduce canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C, mitigating heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4]; the same review cites shade trees improving microclimate stability in Central America (Perfecto and Armbrecht 2003) [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_7]. In Costa Rican coffee, measured shade reduced maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4], and the same tropical synthesis states, citing Avelino et al. 2011, that associated trees buffer air and soil temperature and raise humidity under the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_9]. A CATIE volume reports, from earlier tropical studies, about 2°C cooling under canopy trees averaging 20 m tall compared with a site without trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_2]. The IPCC, citing Ovalle-Rivera et al. 2015 and Schroth et al. 2015, notes that shade trees can ameliorate the rising stand temperatures that will significantly affect arabica coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__heat_str.conditionality: Every unit points to cooling, but the evidence does not state how much that reduces crop or income losses, so the strength is not quantified and the class is slight. Reviews carry their own caveats in the same sentence: IPCC adds that the opposite of shade-tree cooling can also be true [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2], and the coffee review notes that in parts of East Africa excessive shade with heavy rain raised fungal infection risk (Jaramillo et al. 2009) [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_7]. The evidence is crop-specific to coffee and cocoa and reports temperature or microclimate, a component of heat-stress impact, not crop losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]. The 50-year climate-change horizon in the CATIE quote is the cited authors' suggestion, not a measurement [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_2]. The cocoa meta-analysis is weighted towards Ghana (lower-middle income), the Costa Rican measurement is recorded as high income, and the reviews name no country, so the transfer to the LIC/LMIC target is adjacent [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__producti.mechanism: Shade trees over coffee and cocoa have been found both to raise and to lower production. Gains: a coffee meta-analysis found agroforestry reduced the odds of climate-related yield loss (OR = 0.69) and improved continuous outcomes such as yield and bean quality (SMD = +0.42) against conventional systems [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1, ev_crop_yield_patil25_2]; a cocoa meta-analysis found total system yields about ten times higher than in monocultures, and a Bolivian cocoa study cited second-hand found total production three times higher [ev_crop_yield_niether20_2, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_9]; in Ethiopian smallholder coffee, leguminous shade and canopy openness benefited yields, including in the El Niño shock years [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_3]; and second-hand reports cite moderate shade yielding up to 3% more than full-sun coffee, reduced biennial yield oscillation, lower yield variability under diverse shade, intercropped coconut yielding more nuts, nitrogen fixation around 100 kg ha-1 by Erythrina or Inga shade, and in Paraná shaded coffee yielding up to 101.99 kg/ha where the unshaded control yielded zero [ev_crop_yield_villa20_4, ev_yield_stability_montagnini15_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_villa20_12, ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1]. Losses: main-crop yield per hectare was 26% lower in shaded coffee and cocoa than conventional systems and cocoa yields 25% lower than in monocultures [ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_1]; second-hand reports cite cocoa productivity 41% higher in monocultures, a 30% coffee yield reduction once shade was established, 41% fewer coffee fruits under 40 to 60% Erythrina shade, significant productivity reductions under Organic-certified shade coffee, and a cocoa yield ceiling at high carbon storage [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_6, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11, ev_crop_yield_villa20_1, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_4, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_6].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__producti.conditionality: What separates the sides, in the sources' own terms, is first what is counted and second how much shade. The gains in total system output count the by-crops and timber, while the losses are in the main crop alone: the same cocoa meta-analysis reports cocoa yields 25% lower but total system yields about ten times higher [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_2]. Shade density: coffee yields declined under >60% shade with 30 to 60% shade most favourable, fruit set fell under 40 to 60% Erythrina cover, and shaded systems under 30 % cover did not differ from full sun, management intensity driving yield instead [ev_crop_yield_patil25_3, ev_crop_yield_villa20_1, ev_crop_yield_villa20_3]. Drought does not reliably favour shade: in the Ghanaian experiment shade did not prevent the drought-induced cocoa yield decline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2], cited work reports shade trees harming cocoa under severe drought depending on species and tree–cacao water competition pushing yields below open-sun levels [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_3, ev_crop_yield_watts22_8], Bahian cocoa drought losses were unrelated to shade-tree cover and Mexican hurricane harvest losses unrelated to shade management [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6], and diverse shade showed no direct benefit in the El Niño shock [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. Several units find no difference: in a Costa Rican case study no negative yield effect of shade was recorded, coconut yields are not strongly affected by interspace trees except where they block light, galangal yield was unaffected by over-canopy, soil nitrogen did not differ in cocoa systems, and young shaded coffee did not differ in fruiting nodes [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_2, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_2, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_3, ev_soil_nitrogen_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_villa20_2]; the coffee meta-regression found no moderator, shade density included, that significantly explained the variance [ev_crop_yield_patil25_9]. The evidence is crop-specific to coffee, cocoa and coconut; the Ghanaian shade came from nets rather than trees, and the certification loss bundles shade with Organic certification rather than isolating it [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_4]. Many units are earlier studies read second-hand through Portuguese-, Spanish- or French-language reviews [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_6, ev_crop_yield_villa20_1, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_6].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__rural_po.mechanism: Returns to farmers, used here as a proxy for rural poverty, tend to be higher in shaded coffee and cocoa. A meta-analysis found the average net return of shaded systems significantly higher by 23% than conventional systems, with a trend toward a higher benefit-cost ratio (1.66 against 1.44) [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_1, ev_economic_return_jezeer17_2]. Shade also cushions price shocks: in a case cited second-hand, a coffee price crash cut the net revenue of sun-grown coffee far more (30-fold) than of extensive agroforestry (2.9-fold) [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_3], and a farm model for Costa Rica and Guatemala found losses under a 50% coffee price fall were lower for high-shade and diversified systems, with high-shade low-investment farms holding a positive long-run net present value where low-shade farms averaged a negative one [ev_economic_return_lalani24_2, ev_economic_return_lalani24_1]. In Bolivia the return on labour over the years was, by a cited study, almost twice as high in agroforestry as in monoculture, and in Paraná, Brazil a financial model found net present value and benefit-cost index always higher for shaded coffee [ev_economic_return_dsantos23_7, ev_economic_return_robusti17_1]. Among certified coffee farms in Nicaragua, C.A.F.E. Practices certification was associated with higher net income [ev_economic_return_castle21s_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__rural_po.conditionality: The row carries a harm signal: in a farm survey in Guayas, Ecuador, technified monoculture earned the best net margin per hectare ($2323) against $1565 for organic and $484 for traditional cacao agroforestry [ev_economic_return_perezneira16_1, ev_economic_return_perezneira16_2]. Other units find no difference: a pan-tropical cocoa meta-analysis found higher total system production not reflected in higher revenues or net present values [ev_economic_return_niether20_1, ev_household_income_niether20_1], and after Hurricane Stan coffee management had no effect on economic losses in Mexico [ev_economic_return_philpott08_1]. What separates the sides is the comparison: the gains are against sun-grown or low-shade systems and under price shocks, while the losses are against an input-intensive technified monoculture. The certification result is bundled, crediting a certification scheme rather than shade alone [ev_economic_return_castle21s_1], the price-fall and net-present-value comparisons are modelled [ev_economic_return_lalani24_1, ev_economic_return_robusti17_1], and the Bolivian labour-return figure is read second-hand [ev_economic_return_dsantos23_7]. All units are crop-specific to coffee or cocoa except the Bolivian one, and the evidence mostly comes from upper-middle- and lower-middle-income producing countries; returns are proxies for poverty, not poverty itself.

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__soil_ero.mechanism: In shaded coffee, a study on a Costa Rican farm found shade trees reduced sheet erosion by a factor of 2 against full-sun plots [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1], with runoff and erosion attenuated by close to a factor of two [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]; reviews state that shade trees protect soil from erosion through the leaves and branches they add, and that reduced erosion and enhanced infiltration are commonly documented under coffee agroforestry [ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11, ev_erosion_hazard_patil25_6]. After Hurricane Stan in Chiapas, Mexico, coffee farms with more complex vegetation suffered less landslide damage, and the farm area hit by landslides rose as vegetation complexity fell [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_10, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_2, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3]. In Misiones, Argentina, a cited study found the erosion and soil exhaustion of yerba mate monoculture much smaller when the crop is associated with trees [ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__soil_ero.conditionality: The Costa Rican runoff source notes the plot-scale benefit represents little at catchment scale on its soils, and that evidence is high-income [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1]. The Chiapas landslide results come from a single hurricane: the landslide-volume and landslide-size trends were only marginal (P = 0.062), and nearby forest cover did not influence landslide frequency or extent [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4]. The review statements give no size [ev_erosion_hazard_patil25_6, ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11]. The evidence is crop-specific and from upper-middle- and high-income countries, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target. The yerba mate unit is read second-hand from a CATIE edited volume [ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__water_st.mechanism: A pan-tropical meta-analysis found that soils in cocoa agroforestry systems have a significantly lower volumetric water content than full-sun cocoa monocultures, consistent with shade trees competing with cocoa for soil water [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1].
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__water_st.conditionality: The direction rests on a single meta-analysis, crop-specific to cocoa, drawn mostly from lower-middle-income producing countries, and the size of the difference is not encoded [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. Soil moisture enters as a component of water stress; the unit does not measure crop water stress or yield loss in dry periods [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__wind_cyc.mechanism: The row rests on one study of hurricane-hit coffee farms in Soconusco, Chiapas, Mexico, which compared farms of differing vegetation management. It found significant effects of vegetation management on landslides but not on coffee harvest lost, with all farms reporting yield losses between 18 and 40% [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. For the farmer's harvest, shade trees made no measured difference.
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__wind_cyc.conditionality: This is a no-mitigation result from the primary study. A review's second-hand reading of the same study, that more diverse coffee systems suffered less hurricane damage, was dropped from the evidence because the primary does not support it: the difference the study found was in landslides, not in the harvest. The 18 to 40% range is the loss across all farms, not an effect of the trees [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. The unit is crop-specific (coffee) and counts because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; it is a single study in upper-middle-income Mexico, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target, and does not state the hurricane's severity [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6].

agroforestry__shaded_perennial__wind_cyc.mechanism: One study of hurricane-hit coffee farms in Chiapas, Mexico, compared farms of differing vegetation management and found significant effects of vegetation management on landslides but not on coffee harvest lost, with all farms losing between 18 and 40% of harvest [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. Shade trees did not reduce the hurricane's toll on the coffee harvest in that study.
agroforestry__shaded_perennial__wind_cyc.conditionality: The row rests on the primary study's null result, so no mitigation of hurricane harvest loss in shaded coffee is established. A review's second-hand reading of the same study, reporting less damage in more diverse coffee systems, was dropped because the primary does not support it. The 18 to 40% range is the loss on all farms, not an effect of the trees [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. The evidence is coffee-specific, counted under the ruling that shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop, from a single study in upper-middle-income Mexico, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.mechanism: In a severe drought, the area under the most recently planted intensive silvopastoral systems fell by 45 percent across surveyed farms in a Colombian payment-for-ecosystem-services programme [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.conditionality: The loss is in the establishment phase: the source notes established systems were more resilient to drought than traditional pastures [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4]. The evidence is from upper-middle-income Colombia, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.mechanism: A Brazilian review, citing Vosti et al. (1998), states that accidental fire is a constant concern for silvopastoral producers because of the damage it could cause to trees and crops, and that post-fire re-establishment costs could be quite high [ev_fire_hazard_diasf08_3].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is a second-hand comment on producer concern, not a measured loss, from upper-middle-income Brazil, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_fire_hazard_diasf08_3]. A second independent source or one measured finding of fire damage to silvopastoral trees would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.mechanism: A Brazilian review states that in the establishment phase of silvopastoral systems, tree seedlings must be protected from excess solar radiation and wind, as well as trampling, herbivory, weed competition and accidental fire [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__asset_threa.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a sensitivity for this cell: it is one management statement, not a measured loss, wind is one of several establishment-phase threats, and the source is upper-middle-income Brazil, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_diasf08_4]. A second independent source or one measured finding of wind damage to silvopastoral trees would let the cell state a sensitivity.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__biodiversit.mechanism: A global meta-analysis of silvopastoral systems against open pasture reports a pooled biodiversity log response ratio of 0.25 (a 28.4% difference), and the Colombian sustainable-ranching completion report attributes increased species richness and abundance, including many forest-dependent and endangered species, to silvopastoral systems at farm and landscape level [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]. In the Colombian Amazon piedmont, silvopastoral projects significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties, which enters as a forest-cover component [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In Colombia, intensive silvopastoral systems held four times more birds and 35% higher bird species richness than grass monocultures, and ant species richness was 62% higher than in treeless pastures in the same landscape [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__biodiversit.conditionality: The comparator matters: the meta-analysis gain is against open pasture, and the same table reports negative log response ratios for silvopasture compared with native forest, so the benefit applies where trees are added to treeless pasture, not where silvopasture replaces forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1]. The envelope is adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target: the measured project outcome is from upper-middle-income Colombia and the meta-analysis carries no income-group tag, so transfer to low-income pastoral systems is not established by these units [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1]. The Colombian bird and ant figures are earlier studies cited in a CATIE edited volume [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__carbon_sequ.mechanism: Colombian project measurements attribute net CO2 removals to dispersed trees in pasture, live fences and intensive silvopasture, and a preliminary balance reports that greater carbon capture and lower nitrogen losses in intensive silvopastoral systems offset livestock methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2]. Spanish-language reviews add that silvopasture established from degraded woodland increases above- and below-ground carbon stocks and that tree-improved pastures and live fences had a positive effect on the mitigation pillar in a Colombian prioritisation [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6]. Avoided deforestation by silvopastoral projects in the Colombian Amazon piedmont, compared with control properties, also enters as a forest-cover component, with no carbon quantity attached [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems had a carbon storage potential of 1.2 to 4.5 Mg ha-1 yr-1, against less than 1 Mg ha-1 yr-1 in pastures without trees [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__carbon_sequ.conditionality: The Colombian figure is a project total with no per-hectare or per-year denominator, and the other units are cited secondary or expert-prioritisation statements without rates [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6]. The envelope is adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target: the evidence is from upper-middle-income Colombia, high-income Costa Rica and Latin America generally [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__cost_reduct.mechanism: A World Bank completion report for Colombia states that production costs were US$127/ha lower on average under silvopastoral systems than under traditional ranching, attributing the saving to improved animal nutrition, productivity and fertility and lower incidence of animal death and disease [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__cost_reduct.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a class: the figure is second-hand, an estimate the report takes from a Bank-commissioned business case rather than a measurement, and there is no other source to pool with [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7]. A further independent source or a measured cost comparison is what is missing. It comes from upper-middle-income Colombia, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target, and is a recurrent production-cost saving, not an establishment cost [ev_project_cost_cmscr20_7].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__ag.mechanism: Trees were the most important source of animal feed and milk production for agro-pastoralists during drought in a cited Zambian study [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14]. A US silvopasture study lists better water infiltration among the services silvopasture can provide, without linking it to drought [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__ag.conditionality: The Zambian unit is a review citing a single study, and the US unit is a background statement used as a soil-water component proxy for drought [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. The US unit is high-income and outside the LIC/LMIC target; only the Zambian unit (low income) is from the target context [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14]. All units are from agro-pastoral systems [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__al.mechanism: Trees were the most important source of animal feed and milk for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought, and agroforestry in Brazil's semi-arid region had much less year-to-year variation in biomass productivity than conventional systems, attributed mainly to water availability [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6]. A US silvopasture study lists better water infiltration among silvopasture's services [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__al.conditionality: The evidence is adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target: the Zambian unit is low income, the Brazilian and Colombian units are upper-middle income, and the US unit is high income [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. Every unit is reported second-hand or as a background statement (the Zambian finding repeats Chibinga et al. and the Brazilian one Martins et al.), and the US unit is a soil-water component proxy that does not mention drought [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. The Latin American silvopastoral units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__mi.mechanism: The only evidence is a review's second-hand report that in Brazil's semi-arid region agroforestry systems had lower year-to-year variation in biomass productivity over 4 years than conventional systems (for example 16% against 91% for maize plus bean), attributed mainly to water availability [ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__mi.conditionality: This single unit concerns yield stability, not a measured drought impact, and comes from upper-middle-income Brazil, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__pa.mechanism: Trees and fodder shrubs in the pasture keep feed available when grass fails. In Colombia, a review citing Altieri and Nicholls 2013 reports that forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year (Murgueitio et al. 2011) [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought__pa.conditionality: The row rests on Latin American sources only, both upper-middle income or mostly so, outside the LIC/LMIC target, and all its units are earlier studies cited in a Spanish-language review or a CATIE edited volume rather than new measurement [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. The El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The reproduction unit is a general statement without a size [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. No unit reports harm or a null result, but none comes from an African or Asian rangeland.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought_haz.mechanism: Trees were the most important source of animal food and milk production for agro-pastoralists in southern Zambia during drought, and in semi-arid Brazil agroforestry systems showed lower variation in biomass productivity over four years than conventional systems, attributed mainly to water availability [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__drought_haz.conditionality: Both are cited secondary findings without a drought effect size, and the Brazilian unit reports yield stability (coefficients of variation) rather than a drought-year comparison [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6]. Evidence is from low-income Zambia and upper-middle-income Brazil [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__fire__agro_.mechanism: The only study reaching this cell compared silvopasture with non-grazed managed forest in Washington State, USA: silvopasture management reduced grass biomass, litter and duff depth, and the authors conclude that managing overstory, understory and grazing together can reduce fuel loads and potential wildfire risk [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5]. Rotational grazing removes understory biomass and herbaceous surface fuel, and the reduced, more variable overstory density has the potential to reduce fire frequency compared with other land uses [ev_t3_herbaceous_fuel_batcheler24_4, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. Rate of fire spread and burn severity correlate with litter and duff depth in this forest type, which is why the litter reduction matters for fire [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__fire__agro_.conditionality: None of this evidence can set the class. Every comparison is against the unmanaged state, non-grazed managed forest, while this cell asks how silvopasture compares with the open pasture of an agro-pastoral system [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5, ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8]. Against treeless pasture the reading changes: introducing trees adds woody material, litter and duff that open pasture does not have, so having less fuel than a forest does not mean having less fuel than the pasture the practice replaces. Read against that comparator, the fire-spread correlation with litter and duff depth would point to added risk rather than a reduction [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6]. The study is also from a high-income US setting in the Interior Columbia Basin, outside the LIC/LMIC target; only select fuel types fell (1-, 10-, 100- and 1000-h fuels were similar between the management systems), and the fire-frequency statement is a potential effect, not a measurement [ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. What would fill the gap is a fire-risk comparison (fuel load, fire frequency or burn severity) of silvopasture against treeless pasture, ideally in an LIC/LMIC agro-pastoral system.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__flood__all.mechanism: Colombian silvopastoral soils eroded 35.3 percent less than degraded pasture in the Coffee Ecoregion but only 5.4 percent less in the flatter Cesar River Valley [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__flood__all.conditionality: Both figures come from a single World Bank project report comparing silvopasture with degraded pasture rather than conventional pasture, and they measure erosion, a component of flood impact [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__heat_stress.mechanism: Silvopastoral systems cut heat stress in cattle: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it, and eucalyptus–brachiaria systems in Brazil reduced the area at critical animal thermal-comfort levels by 20 to 100% against monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Tree shade in pastures is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover, attributed to less heat stress and more foliage and fruit, and other studies found increases above 15% for cows grazing silvopasture compared with cows in full sun [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__heat_stress.conditionality: Most units are reviews citing earlier studies, and the shade-associated milk and weight-gain figures are associations rather than measured heat-stress losses avoided [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The milk gains mix relief from heat with extra foliage and fruit, so they are not a pure heat-stress effect [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__heat_stress.mechanism: The only evidence is a review's second-hand report that agroforestry systems in Brazil cut the area at critical animal thermal-comfort levels by 20 to 100% compared with monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__heat_stress.conditionality: This is one Brazilian study reported second-hand, from upper-middle-income Brazil, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target, and it measures thermal comfort rather than livestock losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__production_.mechanism: Trees in pasture have been found both to raise and to lower production. Gains, mostly from Latin American intensive silvopasture and shaded pastures: Tree shade in pastures is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain, Brazilian silvopasture gave a higher mean bodyweight gain per animal (512 g day-1) than monoculture (452 g day-1), and tree leaves added about 40 kg ha-1 of nitrogen in a Brazilian semi-arid system [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. In Colombian intensive silvopasture, milk production was 32.1% higher than with the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Intensive silvopasture raises stocking rates up to four times above extensive grazing and with them meat and milk output per hectare [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1]. In Colombia, a Leucaena-based silvopastoral system raised stocking to 4.3 cows ha-1 while eliminating chemical fertiliser [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25%, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are more drought-tolerant and give more stable forage volumes in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During El Niño events, milk production fell by 2.2% in silvopastoral systems against 4.9% in conventional systems [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover and above 15% in silvopasture compared with full sun, and dry-season weight gains were 2 to 5% higher on high tree-density pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Losses come from a global quantitative review of dispersed trees in pasture: pasture yield fell by 20.8% on average against control plots, by a predicted 30% where tree density exceeded 800 trees per hectare, and to below 50% of the control under the oldest trees, while livestock yield fell by 18.6% on average, declining with more trees up to ~300 trees per hectare and with increasing tree age [ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_9, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_10, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_12, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_15, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_16].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__production_.conditionality: The Brazilian and humid-tropic units are cited secondary results, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target; the nitrogen unit is a component rather than a productivity measure [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. Tree density matters: dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. The Latin American livestock units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The Costa Rican units are high-income evidence, and the milk gains attributed to heat relief also reflect extra foliage and fruit [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1]. What separates the sides: tree density and tree age, since in the review newly planted trees had no impact on pasture yield while dense and old stands cut it, and the dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture above also gave less milk than the open field [ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_11, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_10, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_12]; and the system, since the gains are intensive silvopasture with Leucaena shrubs or shaded pasture assessed on milk and weight gain, while the review pools paddock trees and silvopasture against treeless controls. Even in the review a third of livestock paddock years (33%) gained [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14]. The global review's main text gives no country or income-group breakdown, so its losses cannot be placed against the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__silvopastoral__rural_pover.mechanism: Silvopasture raised Colombian farmers' annual income by as much as US$523/ha in a Bank-commissioned business case, participating Colombian Amazon farms saw higher income from animal sales, and Vi Agroforestry advice in Kenya raised the household dietary diversity score by 1.22 [ev_household_income_cmscr20_6, ev_household_income_bur24_1, ev_food_security_castle21s_1]. In Colombia, intensive silvopasture had an operating benefit-cost ratio of 2.8 against 1.34 for a traditional system, and producer income from milk sales was 42.12% higher than under pasture monoculture owing to a higher carrying capacity [ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1, ev_household_income_montagnini15_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__rural_pover.conditionality: Silvopasture income is lower than traditional pasture in the first years after establishment, and on a Nicaraguan farm its net income overtook pasture only in the fifth year [ev_economic_return_diasf08_1, ev_economic_return_diasf08_2]. The largest figure is a modelled upper bound, and the evidence is mainly from upper-middle-income Latin America, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_household_income_cmscr20_6, ev_household_income_bur24_1]. The Colombian sustainable-ranching completion report found no measured poverty reduction at closing, because many silvopastoral systems were still in their establishment phase and project effects could not be separated from drought and other climatic events [ev_rural_poverty_cmscr20_9]. The Colombian ratio and milk-income figures are earlier studies cited in a Spanish-language systematic review and a CATIE edited volume [ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1, ev_household_income_montagnini15_1].

agroforestry__silvopastoral__soil_erosio.mechanism: In Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion, soils under silvopasture lost 12.3 t/ha a year against 19 t/ha for degraded pasture, a mean reduction in erosion of 35.3 percent [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1]. In Costa Rica and Nicaragua, runoff equalled 28-48% of rainfall on pastures without trees against less than 10% in silvopastoral systems [ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1]. Runoff was higher on grass pasture than in tree-dominated fodder banks, so tree cover attenuates runoff and the soil erosion it causes [ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1].
agroforestry__silvopastoral__soil_erosio.conditionality: The Colombian erosion figure is a project measurement against degraded pasture from upper-middle-income Colombia, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1]. The runoff units are earlier studies cited in a CATIE edited volume and a Spanish-language review, entering as components of erosion, and the Costa Rica and Nicaragua figures span high- and lower-middle-income settings [ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1, ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1].

agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk.mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis found agroforestry five and ten times better than controls for runoff and soil loss respectively [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. A pantropical meta-analysis found agroforestry trees reduced soil erosion by 50% against crop monocultures, and stated mechanisms include greater soil cover and structure protecting against raindrop impact, roots aiding infiltration and reducing surface runoff, and live fences lowering runoff velocity; runoff reduction is used as a component [ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_santos25_2, ev_runoff_reduction_watts22_2, ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_5]. WOCAT practitioner ratings add reduced soil loss and surface runoff under assisted natural regeneration in Burkina Faso, and less downstream siltation of ponds and water pans under FMNR in Kenya owing to less wind and water erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_wocat_1358_2017_soil_loss, ev_runoff_reduction_wocat_1358_2017_surface_runoff, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1]. During Hurricane Mitch in October 1998, Honduran farmers practising the Quesungual system suffered less landslide damage than those using traditional slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1]. In Costa Rica and Nicaragua, runoff equalled 28-48% of rainfall on pastures without trees against less than 10% in silvopastoral systems [ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1]. Runoff was higher on grass pasture than in tree-dominated fodder banks, so tree cover attenuates runoff and the soil erosion it causes [ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. Within single sub-practices, live fences of Gliricidia sepium are used to prevent erosion, shade trees attenuate runoff and erosion by close to a factor of two against full-sun plots, and in Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion erosion under silvopasture was 35.3 percent lower than on degraded pasture soils [ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_2, ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1]. In shaded perennial systems, a study on a Costa Rican coffee farm found shade trees reduced sheet erosion by a factor of 2 against full-sun plots [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1], and after Hurricane Stan in Chiapas, Mexico, coffee farms with more complex vegetation suffered less landslide damage [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_10].
agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk.conditionality: The class follows the sub-practice vote, which tempers the pooled result: the large effect sizes come from the cross-family meta-analyses, which hold the strongest result, regeneration-based farmland (FMNR and assisted natural regeneration evidence, the Quesungual landslide result) reads moderate, and boundary planting, shaded perennial systems and silvopasture each read weaker on their own evidence, so the NbS-level class sits at the slight reading shared by boundary planting, shaded perennial systems and silvopasture rather than at the meta-analyses' strong one [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_wvfmnr19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_wocat_1358_2017_soil_loss, ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1, ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6, ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1]. The shade-tree effect represents little at catchment scale on the andisols studied [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]. Silvopasture's weaker reading reflects spread between sites: erosion fell 35.3 percent in Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion but only 5.4 percent in the Cesar River Valley [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The sub-Saharan authors warn the very large effect sizes could reflect publication bias and expect more modest effects with more studies [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. Regreening Africa observed no large overall change in erosion prevalence and found no link between more trees on farm and lower erosion, the FMNR result is participants' reported erosion, and the Nicaraguan hurricane result bundles trees with terraces and contour planting [ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_3, ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_5, ev_erosion_hazard_wvfmnr19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_9]. The WOCAT units are compiler judgements on documented technology sheets, not erosion measurements, and the runoff and siltation ratings enter as components [ev_erosion_hazard_wocat_1358_2017_soil_loss, ev_runoff_reduction_wocat_1358_2017_surface_runoff, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. The Lower Nyando erosion finding is farmer-reported, not measured [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1]. The landslide and runoff results are earlier studies cited in a working paper, a CATIE edited volume and a Spanish-language review; the runoff units enter as components of erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1, ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1, ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. The Chiapas landslide results are crop-specific coffee evidence from a single hurricane, with the landslide-volume and landslide-size trends only marginal (P = 0.062) and no effect of nearby forest cover [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4].

agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__farming.mechanism: In Isiolo County, Kenya, households said that planting trees in a line prevents the soil from being swept away by water [ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1].
agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__farming.conditionality: Both units are farmer statements from Kenyan mixed crop-livestock households, gathered in interviews and focus groups during or after floods, with no measured soil loss or effect size [ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6, ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1].

agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__farming.mechanism: In shaded coffee, a study on a Costa Rican farm found shade trees reduced sheet erosion by a factor of 2 against full-sun plots [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1], with runoff and erosion attenuated by close to a factor of two [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]; reviews state that shade trees protect soil from erosion through the leaves and branches they add, and that reduced erosion and enhanced infiltration are commonly documented under coffee agroforestry [ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11, ev_erosion_hazard_patil25_6]. After Hurricane Stan in Chiapas, Mexico, coffee farms with more complex vegetation suffered less landslide damage, and the farm area hit by landslides rose as vegetation complexity fell [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_10, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_2, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3].
agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__farming.conditionality: The Costa Rican runoff source notes the plot-scale benefit represents little at catchment scale on its soils, and that evidence is high-income [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1]. The Chiapas landslide results come from a single hurricane: the landslide-volume and landslide-size trends were only marginal (P = 0.062), and nearby forest cover did not influence landslide frequency or extent [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4]. The review statements give no size [ev_erosion_hazard_patil25_6, ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11]. The evidence is crop-specific and from upper-middle- and high-income countries, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target.

agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__income_.mechanism: In Costa Rican coffee, a study on a large farm found shade trees reduced sheet erosion by a factor of 2 against full-sun plots [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1], shade trees attenuated runoff and erosion by close to a factor of two [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3], and a review states that shade trees protect soil from erosion and conserve fertility through the leaves and branches they add [ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11].
agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__income_.conditionality: The runoff source notes the plot-scale benefit represents little at catchment scale on these soils [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]. All units are crop-specific coffee evidence from high-income Costa Rica, outside the LIC/LMIC target, and much of it comes from a single farm [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1, ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11]; it should not be transferred to LIC/LMIC systems without local evidence.

agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__income_.mechanism: Under silvopastoral systems in Colombia, mean erosion fell by 35.3 percent in the Coffee Ecoregion (12.3 t/ha a year against 19 t/ha on degraded pasture) and by 5.4 percent in the Cesar River Valley (17.5 against 18.5 t/ha) [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. A Brazilian review explains that agroforestry increases soil cover and improves soil structure, protecting against raindrop impact and reducing wind speed and surface runoff [ev_erosion_hazard_santos25_2]. Runoff was higher on grass pasture than in tree-dominated fodder banks, so tree cover attenuates runoff and the soil erosion it causes [ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. In Chiapas, Mexico, after Hurricane Stan, coffee farms with more complex vegetation suffered less landslide damage, the farm area hit by landslides rose as vegetation complexity fell, and roadside landslides were more numerous where complexity was lower [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_10, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_2, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3]. In Misiones, Argentina, a cited study found the erosion and soil exhaustion of yerba mate monoculture much smaller when the crop is associated with trees [ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1].
agroforestry__soil_erosion_risk__income_.conditionality: The reduction differs widely between the Colombian regions, and the comparator is degraded pasture [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The evidence is from upper-middle-income Latin America, matching this scope row but not LIC/LMIC evidence, and the Brazilian unit is a review statement working through runoff, a component of erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2, ev_erosion_hazard_santos25_2]. The fodder-bank runoff comparison is a review citation without a size, and runoff is a component of erosion [ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. The Chiapas evidence is crop-specific coffee from a single hurricane: the landslide-volume and landslide-size trends were only marginal (P = 0.062), and nearby forest cover did not influence landslide frequency or extent [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4]. The yerba mate unit is read second-hand from a CATIE edited volume and gives no size [ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1].

agroforestry__water_quality_risk.mechanism: The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates downstream siltation as decreased, its compiler noting that less wind and water erosion reduces the siltation of ponds and water pans [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation].
agroforestry__water_quality_risk.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a class: the cell rests on a single compiler judgement on a technology sheet from lower-middle-income Kenya, siltation enters only as a component of water-quality risk, and no unit measures water quality itself [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. A further independent source or a measured water-quality or sediment finding is what is missing.

agroforestry__water_stress.mechanism: The measured soil-water evidence points both ways, and timing and soil depth separate the two sides. On the positive side, a sub-Saharan meta-analysis finds that agroforestry improved infiltration and soil moisture content compared to the control (RR 1.6 for soil moisture, with 70% of soil-moisture observations above RR 1) [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1], and in a German alley-cropping trial in a drought year soil water content remained lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In a Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi, available water content tended to be greater in the gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase, which the authors attribute to increased infiltration and reduced soil evaporation under greater ground cover [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10], and in the second season's May water content in that system was much greater than in all other treatments at depths below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8]. Water use efficiency was also higher in the tree systems in every season, for example 1.97 against 0.15 g of biomass per kg of water for gliricidia + maize against sole maize in 1998/99 [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. On the negative side, under Faidherbia albida parkland in Ethiopia soil moisture in the sub-soil was the least for wheat with tree, intermediate for sole tree and the highest for open field [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]; in cocoa, a pan-tropical meta-analysis found soils under agroforestry significantly lower in volumetric water content than under full-sun monocultures [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]; at Makoka the lower available soil water at the beginning of the cropping season in the tree-based systems suggests that the trees continued to deplete moisture during the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2], the March-to-August decline was most pronounced in the tree-based systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3], water content was slightly lower under gliricidia + maize in the dry season when the trees were left unpruned [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5], and in the first season's May water content under gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea was lower than in all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4]. Trees therefore draw down dry-season and subsoil water, while recharge-season soil water and whole-system water productivity favour them. Several measurements found no difference: topsoil moisture did not vary under Faidherbia [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2], and at Makoka the distribution of water in the profile was generally comparable in all cropping systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1], with no significant treatment effects in the second season, in the second season's October, or in December and January of the third season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]; the authors conclude that gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season does not provoke undue competition for water with associated crops [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11]. WOCAT practitioner ratings add improved water harvesting under assisted natural regeneration in Burkina Faso, and increased water availability under FMNR in Kenya, where the compiler credits greater water retention that raises groundwater levels [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_1358_2017_harvesting_collection_of_water, ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. Rainfall over agricultural land can also shift with continental land cover, increasing with more upwind tree cover [ev_water_regulation_vannoordwijk21_4].
agroforestry__water_stress.conditionality: The sub-practice rows disagree, so this roll-up states the conflict rather than a pooled direction: the meta-analysis carries the cross-family row positive, the Malawi Gliricidia trial (with the German trial) carries the planted silvoarable row positive, and the Faidherbia subsoil depletion and the cocoa soil-water deficit carry the regeneration-farmland and shaded-perennial rows negative [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. The separator is timing and depth: trees deplete soil water through the dry season and below the topsoil, so less may be available when the crop is sown, while recharge-season water and system water productivity favour the tree plots [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10]. Management matters: the Malawi conclusion holds for gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11], and the Ethiopian parkland trees were heavily pruned on farmers' fields [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]. The Makoka water use efficiency figures are total above-ground biomass of the whole system, trees and crops together, per unit of seasonal water use, not grain per unit of water [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1]; the tree biomass inflates the tree-system figures, and the authors caution that soil evaporation and water-table uptake were not measured, so the gap is probably overstated. These units therefore count here, for water stress, and are held out of the production gap because they say nothing about crop yield. The German result counts little: it is a temperate high-income trial whose differences were not significant at all positions, and it measured surface soil only [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. The WOCAT units are compiler judgements on documented technology sheets, not soil-moisture measurements, and stay on water access rather than soil moisture [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_1358_2017_harvesting_collection_of_water, ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. The upwind-rainfall shift is a continental-scale effect, not a field-scale one [ev_water_regulation_vannoordwijk21_4]. Infiltration and groundwater-recharge findings for catchments are carried in the agroforestry catchment water yield rows. The cocoa unit is crop-specific and does not measure crop water stress directly [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1].

agroforestry__water_stress__farming_syst.mechanism: In rainfed cropping the measured evidence points both ways. Trees draw down deeper and dry-season soil water: under Faidherbia albida parkland with wheat in Ethiopia, soil moisture in the sub-soil was the least for wheat with tree, intermediate for sole tree and the highest for open field [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]; in a Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi, the lower available soil water at the beginning of the cropping season in the tree-based systems suggests that the trees continued to deplete moisture during the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2], the March-to-August decline was most pronounced in the tree-based systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3], water content was slightly lower under gliricidia + maize in the dry season when the trees were left unpruned [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5], and in the first season's May water content under gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea was lower than in all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4]. Against this, at Makoka available water content tended to be greater in the gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase, which the authors attribute to increased infiltration and reduced soil evaporation [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10]; in the second season's May that system held much more water than all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8]; and water use efficiency was higher in the tree systems in every season, for example 1.43 against 0.52 g of biomass per kg of water for gliricidia + maize against sole maize in 1997/98 [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. A German alley-cropping trial in a drought year found soil water content remained lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. Several measurements found no difference: topsoil moisture under Faidherbia [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2]; and at Makoka the generally comparable distribution of water in the profile [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1], and no significant treatment effects in the second season, the second season's October, or December and January of the third season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]. The Makoka authors conclude that gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season does not provoke undue competition for water with associated crops [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11].
agroforestry__water_stress__farming_syst.conditionality: What separates the two sides is timing and depth: the trees deplete dry-season and subsoil water, so the crop may start the season with less, while recharge-season soil water and whole-system water productivity favour the tree plots [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10]. Both African studies involve pruned trees, heavily pruned Faidherbia on farmers' fields and gliricidia pruned before and during the crop season; denser or unpruned canopies are not covered [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11]. The water use efficiency figures are total above-ground biomass of trees and crops together per unit of seasonal water use, not grain per unit of water, so the tree biomass lifts the tree-system values [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1]; the authors caution that soil evaporation and water-table uptake were not measured and the gap is probably overstated, and these units count for water stress only, held out of the production gap because they do not measure crop yield. The German trial counts little: it is a temperate high-income site, its differences were not significant at all positions, and it measured surface soil only [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. No study in this cell measures crop water stress itself; soil moisture and water productivity are read as components of it.

agroforestry__water_stress__income_group.mechanism: The measured soil-water evidence points both ways, and timing and soil depth separate the two sides. On the positive side, a sub-Saharan meta-analysis finds that agroforestry improved infiltration and soil moisture content compared to the control (RR 1.6 for soil moisture, with 70% of soil-moisture observations above RR 1) [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. In a Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi, available water content tended to be greater in the gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase, which the authors attribute to increased infiltration and reduced soil evaporation under greater ground cover [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10], and in the second season's May water content in that system was much greater than in all other treatments at depths below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8]. Water use efficiency was also higher in the tree systems in every season, for example 1.97 against 0.15 g of biomass per kg of water for gliricidia + maize against sole maize in 1998/99 [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. On the negative side, under Faidherbia albida parkland in Ethiopia soil moisture in the sub-soil was the least for wheat with tree, intermediate for sole tree and the highest for open field [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]; in cocoa, a pan-tropical meta-analysis found soils under agroforestry significantly lower in volumetric water content than under full-sun monocultures [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]; at Makoka the lower available soil water at the beginning of the cropping season in the tree-based systems suggests that the trees continued to deplete moisture during the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2], the March-to-August decline was most pronounced in the tree-based systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3], water content was slightly lower under gliricidia + maize in the dry season when the trees were left unpruned [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5], and in the first season's May water content under gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea was lower than in all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4]. Trees therefore draw down dry-season and subsoil water, while recharge-season soil water and whole-system water productivity favour them. Several measurements found no difference: topsoil moisture did not vary under Faidherbia [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2], and at Makoka the distribution of water in the profile was generally comparable in all cropping systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1], with no significant treatment effects in the second season, in the second season's October, or in December and January of the third season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]; the authors conclude that gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season does not provoke undue competition for water with associated crops [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11]. WOCAT practitioner ratings add improved water harvesting under assisted natural regeneration in Burkina Faso, and increased water availability under FMNR in Kenya, where the compiler credits greater water retention that raises groundwater levels [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_1358_2017_harvesting_collection_of_water, ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability].
agroforestry__water_stress__income_group.conditionality: Within low- and lower-middle-income evidence the sides still disagree: the sub-Saharan meta-analysis and the Malawi Gliricidia trial sit on the positive side, while the Faidherbia subsoil depletion in Ethiopia and the cocoa soil-water deficit sit on the negative side [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. The separator is timing and depth: trees deplete soil water through the dry season and below the topsoil, so less may be available when the crop is sown, while recharge-season water and system water productivity favour the tree plots [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10]. Management matters: the Malawi conclusion holds for gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11], and the Ethiopian parkland trees were heavily pruned on farmers' fields [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]. The Makoka water use efficiency figures are total above-ground biomass of the whole system, trees and crops together, per unit of seasonal water use, not grain per unit of water [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1]; the tree biomass inflates the tree-system figures, and the authors caution that soil evaporation and water-table uptake were not measured, so the gap is probably overstated. These units therefore count here, for water stress, and are held out of the production gap because they say nothing about crop yield. The WOCAT units are compiler judgements on documented technology sheets, not soil-moisture measurements, and stay on water access rather than soil moisture [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_1358_2017_harvesting_collection_of_water, ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. Infiltration and groundwater-recharge findings for catchments are carried in the agroforestry catchment water yield rows. The cocoa unit is crop-specific and does not measure crop water stress directly [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1].

agroforestry__waterlogging__all.mechanism: The only evidence is a review's second-hand report that under waterlogging in Punjab, India, agroforestry systems had higher evapotranspiration than sole crops, indicating greater removal of excess water from the soil and a better soil environment for plant growth [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9].
agroforestry__waterlogging__all.conditionality: This single unit is from lower-middle-income India, within the LIC/LMIC target, and reports evapotranspiration rather than a measured yield or livelihood effect [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9]. The evidence is too thin to say whether, or how far, agroforestry changes this impact: a second independent source or one measured finding is needed before a direction can be stated.
